The hon. member spoke to me some time ago about his intention to make an inquiry about the uncompleted boundary line between Ontario and Quebec in the St. Lawrence area. I had the opportunity to see the records of the department and I find that the correspondence goes as far back as February 1938, when a series of questions was placed on the order paper and answered by Hon. Since I became associated with this department there has been further correspondence. On December 8, 1953, I received a letter from Hon. Lionel Chevrier, then minister of transport, pointing out the urgency of having this boundary survey completed. Following receipt of his letter, I wrote to the ministers responsible for boundary survey work in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec. The last paragraph of my letter reads as follows:
You may wish to renegotiate the matter with the province of Quebec (or the province of Ontario), towards the completion of the survey for the demarcation of the line. I can assure my hon. friend that, as soon as requests are received from the provinces of Ontario and Quebec for the completion of this boundary survey, our department will act immediately.

speakeroldname: Hon. Milton F. Gregg (Minister of Labour) moved
speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EQUAL PAY TO FEMALE EMPLOYEES FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide equal pay for female employees as compared with male employees of the same employer, for identical or substantially identical work in federal works, undertakings or businesses; and to provide further under the enforcement procedure for the appointment of referees who may be paid such allowances and expenses as may be approved by the treasury board.
Motion agreed to and the house went into committee, Mr. Robinson (Simcoe East) in the chair.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour
subtopic: PROVISION FOR EQUAL PAY TO FEMALE EMPLOYEES FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, this resolution, item No. 11 on today's order paper, has now been on the order paper for quite a long time, and I can assure the committee at once that, with the exception of nine days at the end of June, I have been ready and anxious to bring it forward for consideration. However, it has been unavoidably delayed and as the time of unavoidable delay has stretched out in length the statement I planned to make at the resolution stage has conversely become shorter and shorter. I am sure that the committee will agree with that point of view this morning.
The idea contained in the resolution goes back for some years in Canadian history. As the hon. member for Rosetown-Biggar suggested in his speech in the debate on the speech from the throne, the idea was voiced in this chamber about 20 years ago by the then hon. member for Grey-Bruce, Miss Agnes Macphail. But to come down to more recent years, I am sure that all members of the house and many others outside the house have been impressed by the aggressive campaign that has been waged for this idea by the hon. member for Hamilton West. I pay tribute this morning in unstinted fashion to the value of the hon. lady's work in assisting in the crystallization of public opinion in this regard. Perhaps not so obvious but nevertheless effective has been the persistent influence for action in this field brought to bear by the hon. member for Timiskaming.
I could very well go on and speak of encouragement for a step such as this from women's organizations, from the Canadian Labour Congress or those congresses that are now part of the Canadian Labour Congress and from women and, yes, men too in this and the other chamber of parliament, and from outside.
In recent years, especially during and since the last war, an increasing number of women
30, 1956	6659
Female Employees Equal Pay have joined our Canadian labour force. Their record shows clearly that women's work is not inferior to the work of men. It would be presumptuous this morning for me to attempt to argue that point. That fact goes without saying. This unquestioned fact has tended to focus attention on the relationship of the earnings of men as compared with those of women doing the same work. In other years when my friend the hon. member for Hamilton West has brought her bill forward I have pointed out that the Canadian government, for quite a long time, has favoured this principle of equal pay. It had made the principle effective. The salaries paid to the classified civil service of Canada have been determined by the content of the job completely irrespective of sex. Also, with respect to our prevailing rate employees across the country, there has been inaugurated the practice of setting the rate for the particular job or of setting the wage classification whether the work has been done by a man or a woman. However, when that was done, it was quite another matter as to whether or not legislation was desirable dealing with the rate of pay of women in private business or private industry that comes under federal labour laws or under federal jurisdiction. For instance, to go beyond our own boundaries, it was observed that in so highly organized a country as the United Kingdom there is as yet no legislation dealing fully with the question of equal pay even in their public service. As was pointed out last year by my hon. friend, in 1955 the United Kingdom adopted a scheme applicable to the civil service. By it the scale for women in the nonindustrial civil service is being steadily increased by seven bites or by seven annual instalments so that by the year 1960 or 1961 women will be on an equal basis with men with respect to rates of pay. The United Kingdom so far at least has maintained that equal pay legislation is not appropriate to their system of private industry. At least they have not yet carried into effect legislation to bear upon that matter.
In the United States, although seventeen states have put into force legislation along this line and although sundry resolutions and private bills have been presented before one or the other of the houses of congress, congress as a whole has not passed legislation covering women in the federal field.
Nevertheless this morning I propose that we initiate federal action in Canada. Last year and previously I promised the house that we would give consideration to the matter and that we would consult with those organizations especially interested in the application of that principle. We have done that.

Female Employees Equal Pay We have done that quite fully. As a result, we have come to the conclusion that legislative proposals especially adapted to the nature of employment under federal jurisdiction should now be recommended to parliament.
I feel sure that it can be administered. In view of the past record or the past experience that I have had of the co-operation of employers in connection with other federal legislation administered by my department, I am confident that those employers will voluntarily bring their practices into compliance with the spirit of this proposed legislation.
This resolution forecasts a measure designed primarily to promote equal pay for women. In the measure that will come before us after the resolution I do not think we should try to be in any sense legalistic perfectionists, but rather that we should try to provide legislation that is simple, that we are quite sure will work and that will promote the object in view. Then, after it is under way, experience only will show us where we should cross the t's and dot the i's.
I want to emphasize the importance of a national standard of equal pay for women on two counts. The first is as evidence of recognition of the important part that women have to play and are playing in our Canadian economy. The second.-and this is a very important one-is the encouragement of them to take an even larger share in the responsibility for Canada's rapid growth. At present there are about a million and a quarter women in our labour force in Canada this mid-summer; that is the total in our entire labour force, in all the activities, whether they come under federal or provincial jurisdiction. Of that number, approximately 73,000 are employed in activities that are under the federal jurisdiction. And I am quite sure that our economy, in the buoyant state in which it is at the present time, needs more of these women who feel that they can come into the labour force. We need them to help out in Canada's development, and for those who are in the labour force and who may come into it I am very glad to propose this resolution as a recognition of the value of their contribution to the growth of Canada. I have pleasure in moving this resolution, Mr. Chairman.

subtopic: PROVISION FOR EQUAL PAY TO FEMALE EMPLOYEES FOR EQUAL WORK
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, first of all I would like to thank the minister for his kind remarks, and in doing so I would like to thank all the members of this house who in past years have supported this type of legislation, both in their remarks in this house and on two occasions by their votes. It was significant that the votes on this type of legislation in past years crossed party lines. The legislation received the support, both in speeches and by votes of all parties in this

house. I believe that that support, as witnessed in this chamber, was in some measure responsible for the government's serious consideration of the principle and its introduction of the legislation which we shall have before us shortly.
I should like to say also that the minister is quite correct when he refers to those persons outside of this chamber who have given consistent support to the principle of equal pay legislation over a period of many years, and I am sure it must be extremely gratifying to them. I mention in particular the federation of business and professional women which has been most outspoken and which has worked hard to have this type of legislation introduced in all legislatures in Canada. I mention also the women who belong to political organizations of all parties who have consistently supported this type of legislation and by reason of their support have succeeded in having this principle accepted by their political parties and incorporated into political platforms. When I make that remark, I think of course of my own party. But I also pay tribute to the women of all other political parties who have used their influence in this regard. Of course, I cannot help but pay tribute to the pioneer in representation of women in this parliament, Miss Agnes Mac-phail, who was always a champion of the things which she considered to be fair and equal for all people.
I think I would have to take a little exception to the minister's remarks with reference to the United Kingdom because, although, as he says, there has been no legislation there, the schemes to introduce the principle of equal pay have extended into many fields. Apart from the nonindustrial employees to whom he referred, those generally in the civil service, both at the local government level and at the higher level, have been covered in schemes which have been brought down, the first of which, of course, for civil servants in general took effect in February, 1955, and the second one on the local government level in July of last year. But in addition to that the scheme also is currently in operation covering school teachers in England and Wales, which came into effect in May of last year and a further one covering teachers in Scotland, which carrte into effect in September. The principle is now being extended to the nurses and to rail transport workers. Therefore it is gradually growing in the United Kingdom, as it is elsewhere.
In Canada, of course, with regard to the provinces, two more provinces passed legislation this year covering equal pay, namely, Manitoba and Nova Scotia. They are the most recent converts to the principle. This

now brings to five the number of provinces in Canada which have adopted equal pay legislation.
The minister also remarked on the United States and the fact that 16 states and Alaska now have equal pay legislation. Three of these adopted the legislation in 1955, of course; and, despite the fact that the minister points out the United States has not yet adopted legislation, it is significant that this year, in his state of the union message, President Eisenhower stressed the point that equal pay for equal work, regardless of the sex, is, in his words, "a matter of simple justice".
The numbers of women who have been engaged in paid employment have increased steadily in Canada, as they have in all other countries, and there have been improvements from time to time in the matter of remuneration, in working hours and in general conditions; but, as was pointed out in an article which appeared on this subject in the Christian Science Monitor, those improvements have hardly kept pace with the importance of the woman worker in the labour force.
The minister has said that in Canada we have now one and a quarter million women engaged in paid employment. The latest figures which I was able to procure are for May of this year. They show a force of 1,312,000 or, as the minister has said, slightly over the million and a quarter mark. They represent well over 23 per cent of the entire labour force of 5,664,000.
As time has gone on and as the numbers of women engaged in employment have increased, there has been a change in the wage structure in all countries, and this is reflected in the report which appears in the International Labour Review of March, 1956. After an exhaustive study and the citing of some very interesting figures the whole article concludes with these words:
Since the narrowing of differentials has taken place during a period of rising real wages during which conditions have improved in the lower-paid occupations and industries more than in others, the basic trend can be considered as one "levelling-up". Thus the net result has been not only improved conditions for wage earners as a whole but also greater equality between occupational and industry groups and between the sexes.
When one speaks of equality in the field of remuneration one necessarily becomes curious as to the number of persons who are in the various pay groups and therefore I referred to the tax statistics for 1955 published under the authority of the Minister of National Revenue. I find that for the taxation year 1953, which is fairly recent, according to the statistics which are available, in
Female Employees Equal Pay the wage group under $2,300 the number of female taxpayers greatly exceeds the number of male taxpayers. This points up the fact that a great many women must be receiving less remuneration for their services than men for the reason that there are, as we have said before, only 23-2 and in 1953 it was less than that. In 1953 about 22 per cent of the entire labour force were women, yet in the earning group of taxpayers earning under $2,300 female taxpayers greatly outnumber male taxpayers.
Of all taxpayers we have a total of 814,340 males and 708,150 females, a difference of about 124 per cent in the number of taxpayers and a difference of 78 per cent in the number of persons. This serves to point up the fact that whereas women represent only about one-quarter of the labour force, when it comes to paying taxes they greatly increase in importance. I hope the Minister of National Revenue is conscious of this fact.
I should point out, Mr. Chairman, if I did not mention it previously that the figures I have just quoted are for single persons. When we move into the field of persons who are taxed as single but who are supporting one or more dependents we find that in the male classification there are 122,490 and in the female classification there are 30,360, something around 25 per cent as compared with 22 per cent of women engaged in paid employment.
It appears that the alibi, if you like that expression, which has frequently been given for refusal to consider equal pay, that women after all are not the supporters of dependents and consequently need not be considered as requiring the same amount of remuneration as men, rather falls short of the mark. It is interesting to observe as these tables come out year by year that the number of women who are supporting dependents increases as the years go by. I will not weary the house by quoting further statistics because they are readily available in this volume for anyone who wishes to examine them.
This is a principle which has long been given lip service by all political parties and in most countries. It is gratifying that we now have at least a recognition in concrete form of this principle in this house.
The minister has said that in approaching a study of the legislation which will be before us shortly we should not be too legalistic, and I think that is probably true. On the other hand, those of us who are keenly interested in this type of legislation could perhaps be forgiven if we have a desire to look for the loopholes which might exist in this legislation. I do not suppose any one of us who

Female Employees Equal Pay studied the legislation we passed last year revising the Unemployment Insurance Act ever thought the interpretation which was later given to it would result in so many disqualifications. It should be a lesson to all of us not only to watch the actual phraseology of the legislation itself but also to be wary of the regulations which may be put into effect and the interpretation which may be given both to the regulations and to the actual legislation.
Therefore, Mr. Chairman, I would just like to make the comment here that regardless of the perfection or lack of it of the bill which may be brought down, if the minister's department is not prepared to give to that legislation a sympathetic interpretation and to provide regulations which will make the working of that legislation flexible and effective, then the legislation itself will be worth nothing. I am sure the minister agrees with me in this regard and I hope that, after the experience we have had in the other fields, he himself will be particularly cautious and will be on the lookout for anything which may be introduced at the regulation and interpretation stage which would nullify the effect of the legislation.
It is not my intention to continue beyond the few remarks I have made today because I am anxiously awaiting the terms of the bill itself. However, I would like to say that in the minister's remarks he rather implied that this legislation was probably a reward for participation in the labour force for the work which women had done and are continuing to do and that it will perhaps be an inducement to increasing numbers of them to enter gainful employment. I do not think any of them wants rewards. What they want is their just due. I would just like to conclude my remarks by again referring to the comment of President Eisenhower which I quoted at the outset of these few words, that this legislation is simply a matter of justice.

Mr. Chairman, I do not propose to enter into any discussion as to whether, this legislation is a matter of recognition or of reward. Our feelings at this time are somewhat akin to those of the minister in that we have a certain disposition to say, "Me too," to the hon. member for Hamilton West who has quite properly, because she is a woman member of this house, carried the ball for

some time in connection with this particular piece of legislation. As has been pointed out by the hon. member for Hamilton West and the Minister of Labour, this legislation is simply carrying forward what was proposed first of all by the first woman member of this house, the late Miss Agnes Macphail. I think it might be worth while if I put on the record the precise terms of the resolution we have before us because, as far as I can recall, neither of the two speakers who preceded me has done this. The resolution reads: That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide equal pay for female employees as compared with male employees of the same employer, for identical or substantially identical work in federal works, undertakings of businesses; and to provide further under the enforcement procedure for the appointment of referees who may be paid such allowances and expenses as may be approved by the treasury board.
As the minister pointed out, this resolution has been on the order paper since the beginning of this session. One cannot help but recall something that occurred in this chamber not very long ago, of course not while the house was in session. I do not know whether the Minister of Labour was among the hon. members who stayed behind the curtains on the occasion when this chamber was filled with representatives of the business and professional women's associations, but I think there were many of us who thought that perhaps the terms of this resolution should be somewhat revised to make sure that discriminations which have existed in the past may not be in effect in reverse in the future. It might well be that some time in the future a minister of labour for Canada might have to make some amendments to the act along those lines. Perhaps I should say that if that crisis should arise we could hope that it would be a woman minister of labour who would be introducing those amendments.
When this legislation is boiled down it is actually a further recognition of the fact that there are certain rights and dignities which should belong to all people regardless of their sex, colour or creed, as part of the recognition that they are human beings equal before God. For that reason I along with the other members of the C.C.F. group in this house hail the introduction of such legislation as something of a milestone in that direction; and certainly we will be prepared to give full and careful consideration to the details of the bill when we have it before us. If we feel there are ways in which it can be improved to further the purposes for which it is designed we may have some suggestions to make at that time.
It is hardly necessary for me to say that we are most wholeheartedly in support of

this proposal. However, in saying that, we recognize, as has the minister, that legislation is not a complete answer to any form of discrimination or intolerance, that there are limitations to what can be done by legislation in this particular field. Those of us in this house and Canadians generally should not feel that once this bill becomes law the battle against this particular form of discrimination is at an end.
In saying that, I might draw to the attention of the minister an example which I consider indicates the real value of this type of legislation. The union, in an industrial plant with which I happened to be familiar and which had been certified as the bargaining agent, had been endeavouring to have a certain policy of racial discrimination abolished in the plant. The question had been discussed and negotiations opened in various ways over a period of some years, but they were unsuccessful as far as the union was concerned. Gradually the union had narrowed down the area of bargaining until it was felt that this matter might soon be resolved to their satisfaction. At that time the government passed the Canada Fair Employment Practices Act and while that act had no jurisdiction over this particular plant it proved to be the straw that broke the camel's back. The mere fact that the parliament of Canada had given recognition to that particular principle, and by that legislation had said in effect that this form of discrimination should be abolished, was sufficient to bring home to that employer the fact that this was something which should no longer be tolerated in Canadian life.
I feel that that probably will be the most important result of this legislation. After all in many parts of this far-flung country, and the parts I know best are a long way from here, what this parliament does in matters of this kind is regarded with a great deal of respect. The impact upon the thinking of the people of the passage of a bill of this kind is perhaps greater than we may be prone to think. That perhaps is one reason why we regret that other pieces of legislation which we feel would reduce inequities and intolerances have not received the recognition by the government we would like to have them receive.
I think we have to recognize that, if we pass legislation, that becomes the law which should be enforced. That is why I am glad to see that there is reference in the resolution to an enforcement procedure, and it is to be hoped that that procedure will have some teeth in it. While the legislation will have some impact, nevertheless we all recognize that there is always a minority who
30, 1956
Female Employees Equal Pay seem to have no appreciation of proper human values. That is perhaps the strongest argument for putting into legislative form such principles as are involved in this resolution. To those people who have no regard for the dignity and the rights of people, the threat of a possible prosecution very often is enough to bring them into line. Few people like to have to appear in the courts and to receive the publicity that is attached to a conviction for a discriminatory practice. Therefore the fact that there is going to be this law with teeth in it, even though one may recognize that by clever arguing certain loopholes may be found, the mere fact that it is there and that prosecution is possible will in itself have a salutary effect in the particular field that this legislation is designed to cover.
One of the further effects of this type of legislation is that it is going to be a step forward in the matter of the proper and careful evaluation of what is involved in a certain job category. It is going to mean, I think, a further step in the direction of the setting of wage levels on a proper and- though I hesitate to use the word-scientific basis, because I think we all realize that until fairly recent times the wages paid to either male or female employees have been set on rather haphazard lines. In some cases it was a matter of as much or as little as the traffic would bear, and a great many inequities have resulted because of that.
I think we all are aware that in recent years there has been some movement towards the setting of standards which are just and equitable having in mind all the various factors that are involved in the content of a certain job. I think that this legislation will serve to put the movement forward another step so that jobs will be paid for on the basis of what they are really worth and not in each particular instance because of the fact that perhaps an employer is able to exert more pressure upon a woman than upon a man and all those factors that have come into play in the past.
Without further prolonging my remarks at this time I simply want to say again that I am quite happy that the minister is bringing forward this legislation at this time. I have been a little worried once or twice during the session that we might have seen this session coming to a close without this bill being brought forward, and I am glad to see that we have it on the way.

speechtext:
We in this group also welcome the resultion at this time. I must admit that I felt somewhat as did the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that possibly we would be drawing near to the close of the session and

Female Employees Equal Pay the resolution would die on the order paper. We are pleased to see it here now.
The hon. member tor Hamilton West suggested that there were only five provinces which had similar legislation on their statute books. I wonder whether she has given any consideration to the fact that some provinces do not find it necessary to pass legislation for equal pay for equal work, since they have no discrimination in their present legislation that would make it necessary. I am thinking specifically of the province of Alberta, where I am told they have no necessity for this type of legislation, there being no discrimination. The teachers' salaries are on an equal basis and I understand that the other civil servants and other employees of the provincial government are likewise and therefore the legislation is not needed.
In my own province of British Columbia the government saw fit to pass such legislation a year or two ago. I must say at this time that again I would agree with the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, and I am pleased to see some teeth put into this legislation, which will make its implementation possible. It is useless having legislation unless one can guarantee that it is going to be implemented, and that might be one of the problems with which we shall have to deal more specifically at a later date.
The principle of equal pay for equal work is, I think, one that should be recognized throughout this nation as possible in every industry. It gives me some concern and wonder as to why we did not include the word "sex" in our revision of the employment act when we were redrafting it last year. I think the suggestion' was made that in the fair employment section of the act, if we introduced the word "sex", there should be no discrimination and that that would take care of this situation and give a guarantee against the need for this type of legislation in this country.
The fact that our government has taken the lead in this, as well as the many provincial governments that have done so earlier, is desirable. It may be somewhat of a guide to employers in the future to arrive at a decision as to whether further legislation should not be brought in or that they themselves could organize to see that labour across this country as a whole is treated the same. For instance, I find on examination that there is a great deal of discrepancy in the wages paid in different parts of this country, not as between male and female necessarily but as between males themselves.
I have an example in mind in Saint John, New Brunswick, with which I am sure the minister is familiar. The mill workers begin


in the lumber business at a beginning wage of 70 or 75 cents per hour, I am told. In my own province, in New Westminster, the beginning wage is $1.60 per hour, and the cost of living is very similar in those cities.
Whilst we have legislation here respecting equal pay for equal work by men and women, I wonder whether some day we shall not find it necessary to introduce legislation of a similar nature covering a greater field than we have now. I could cite another example in the case of check-out girls in supermarkets in the city of Ottawa. I find that in this city the maximum wage paid a girl employed on that work is something like $40 per week. The maximum wage in the city of New Westminster for girls in similar employment is $55 per week. That is their take-home pay, I understand, and since I received that figure there has been an upward trend from that through negotiation in British Columbia. The fact is that in New Westminster the beginning wage paid to ladies employed as check-out girls in supermarkets is $39 per week, which compares with the maximum wage in Ottawa of $40 per week for the same type of work. There may be instances where girls may get more than that but generally speaking that is the wage paid. The universal adoption of this type of legislation could well result in the greatest sociological change of the past half century so far as the Canadian people are concerned if the principle of equal pay for equal work is recognized universally. It would then remain for an employer to decide whether he should employ a man or a woman and he would have to take into consideration not just the fact of having to pay an equal wage but what the results will be on his industry by paying women the same wage.
In many provinces women have special privileges so far as their work is concerned. For instance, there is the fact that these girls who work in stores are not permitted to carry boxes weighing more than a certain amount. The same regulations do not apply to the male. Therefore when an employer decides whether he will employ a male or a female he will, of course, have to give that point some consideration. I am fully aware that that factor does not apply specifically to this legislation because it relates to work over which the federal government has no jurisdiction, but at the same time I cannot help but feel that the adoption of such legislation is bound to have its impact upon the demands of labour throughout the country, and that fact should be recognized.
I can see that the result can' well mean that wherever possible women may be forced

to go back to doing housework and that if the employment they seek is going to call for exactly the same wage the employer is going to decide that he cannot get the same or identical service from women because of the special privileges granted under provincial rights and that they should not receive the same pay. Therefore he will employ men instead. That might be to the advantage of the nation as a whole. I am satisfied that women can hold their end up pretty well if need be. As one who has employed them for some time in business, my experience is that they are quite capable of doing certain jobs. There are fields where that does not hold true and where women have been employed in the past. I am reminded of a quotation from Milton-I forget from which sonnet it comes-

No, Milton. "They also serve
who only stand and wait." I believe that the payment to such a person should compare with the payment to the person who is fully employed because just standing around doing nothing is sometimes harder than to be doing something. It is important that we should recognize that the adoption of this type of legislation may materially affect the adoption of similar types of working conditions in industry generally. Some have them today. In recent years I find there has been a great change in employment in my own province in the case of the union that makes agreements with management in the lumbering business. A few .years ago a great number of women were employed in the plywood factories in my riding. Today we find there are very few because they are incapable of doing the same type of work. Yet they receive the same pay as men because there is no discrimination in the take-home pay.
I think the legislation is possibly to the advantage of both the male and the female. What its final result will be is difficult to decide. I wonder whether the adoption of the legislation will cause concern to labour and industry and may not result finally in a complete return to the apprenticeship system under which industry feels that just because a person is employed at the same job does not necessarily mean that they will be given exactly the same return for their work. There may be a move to adopt the apprenticeship system whereby industry can get certain employees for less money and still attain the main objective of getting the work done.
Possibly the legislation may result in a policy of piece work payment similar to what was so common in the 1920's. It may mean
Female Employees Equal Pay that we will have a guaranteed wage plus the adoption of the principle of people being paid for the exact number of pieces of work they do or it may even bring about-and this might be most desirable-a sharing of profits between industry and employees. Whether this type of legislation will solve the labour problems of today is debatable. Whether it will result in lowering the cost of living is debatable. It well might do so because I can see that when you pay equal wages for the work done and get the same amount of work out of each individual the result may be that a greater amount of work will be accomplished. The result will naturally be greater production at the same cost or a very slight increase in cost because the difference in wages is not too great today. The result might be advantageous in its effect upon the cost of living. On the other hand, if industry generally is made subject to similar legislation the result might be the opposite effect.
There is one thought that does give me some concern. Are women prepared to accept the disadvantages as well as the advantages of this type of legislation? Today they very definitely receive special privileges either written into contracts or observed by management as such. Just because the employee is a lady she may be given certain definite advantages that are not available to the man. However, there is another factor, the fact that competition may mean, as I suggested earlier, the possibility of non-acceptance of the lady in employment and the giving of the particular job to a man. That would mean that the ladies of the country would of necessity be forced into doing more housework. I am not suggesting for a moment that that is of necessity the result. I am just wondering whether that is not a possibility. I think they are prepared to accept their responsibility and to give up any few small advantages they have today for this type of legislation. I am satisfied that it is a step in the right direction. I am prepared to accept it and I am satisfied that each member of our group is.
On the other hand, I wonder whether men are prepared to accept the challenge of women who see here a material advantage, and I would caution all men to look to their laurels. Women are marching forward. They may become the breadwinners for their families and dishpan hands may be our lot.

Mr. Chairman, I of course am very pleased, as all women in Canada must be, that this principle is to become a matter of legislation. I was interested in the remarks made by the hon. member for New Westminster. He has indeed pointed up a problem which may arise, that under certain

However, that is the strongest argument for having the legislation drafted in such a way that it is up to the women themselves to lay the complaint before action is taken. Under such circumstances I have reason to believe that would be the type of legislation we would have because the minister has expressed himself as being against having someone go around, make an inspection and raise the issue when no complaint is laid by the individuals concerned. The women are not too foolish and I am quite sure they would not lay complaints if they felt that the economy of the small industry, or whatever the case might be in the small community, would be jeopardized.
Along that same line I have some figures with regard to complaints laid under the Ontario legislation. That legislation became effective on January 1, 1952. I have the figures here up to March, 1954. There were 122 persons involved in the complaints but only 10 employees. That is in a period of something over two years. However, that does not mean that is all the passing of the legislation accomplished because, of course, once the legislation became law it was possible for groups of women-and I am thinking of school teachers and other large groups such as that-to get equal pay without being obliged to lay the matter before the investigating board. Furthermore, there may be many other instances-and I believe this to be true-where perhaps an obvious injustice exists and where women for some reason are loath to take the matter before the authorities. However, there is nothing that we can do here to take care of that situation. It is up to women to talk to women and to encourage them to get justice.
Now that we have every reason to believe that the legislation will be passed shortly, women's groups and individuals throughout Canada are concerning themselves with what the wording of the act might be. We were criticized mildly either for delaying the passing of the bill presented by the hon. member for Hamilton West or the government not bringing in one earlier. The minister has told you that he wanted the legislation to be effective and that he did not think the wording suggested or the wording in some other act was perhaps the best that could be obtained. The women's organizations and others are concerned over just what that legislation might be.
I should like to read you some comments made by the late Senator Taft when this matter was before a special committee of which he was the head. You all know of the great study he made of labour conditions. 

Bills of this nature were introduced over there in the United States at approximately the same time as the late Miss Agnes Macphail introduced one here and they have been before the United States senate and congress ever since then. In discussing the matter in a committee the senator had this to say:
No basis is provided for determining what jobs are comparable in character, what jobs require comparable skills, what is a comparable quality of work, or what operation is similar to another. A zealous administrator, given this blank cheque, could find quite different types of work to be comparable in character .	.	. Many factors go
into the determination of the wage rate. The terms "work of a comparable character" and jobs which require "comparable skills" are so general and vague that the administrator of the law under such an ambiguous grant of power could destroy the sound wage structure which an employer had worked for years to perfect. Can any employer determine with certainty that he is in compliance? There are degrees of similarity between various jobs and the task of measuring accurately the "skill", "care", "energy", "working conditions", etc. that goes into a given job and at the same time predict that a Department of Labour investigator would make the same valuation is an impossible one.
Then Senator Donnell is quoted at the same hearing as having said:
I think there are few representative of labour or management who would claim that it is possible to develop a job-evaluation system which could be depended upon in all cases to produce fair and mutually acceptable determinations of "work of comparable character on jobs the performance of which requires comparable skills".
Then he goes on to speak further on the same subject. These are the very words, or are almost the identical work words which were in the private bill presented by the hon. member for Hamilton West.
Of course I do not know, nor do you, what will be the words in the bill that will be presented by the minister tomorrow, I believe. But I think the hon. member for Hamilton West said in effect that no matter what those words may be, it will be the sympathetic administration of this act which will create the greatest good. I am not too much concerned about the words. I hope they will please most of the women's groups. However, I am reasonably confident that we shall have sympathetic administration.

As has been indicated in the remarks that have already been made, it will be necessary to wait until the legislation is before us until we see the exact wording of the measure that we are all anxious to support. I want to point out, however, that the introduction of this resolution represents a very gratifying and, I should think, very heart-warming reward to the hon. member for Hamilton West for the efforts she has made now for

many years to bring this matter to the attention of the house and of the people of Canada.
The hon. member for Hamilton West brought similar legislation forward in 1953, again in 1954 and again in 1955. It was not debated or voted upon in 1953 but there were debates and votes in 1954 and 1955. On each occasion the government saw fit to oppose this legislation. I am not going to elaborate on that point now. We welcome the fact that the government has adopted this principle. Already it is in effect in five of the provinces of Canada and it has been giving satisfaction where it is in operation. One of the things that I should like to mention is the fact that, far from placing the men at a disadvantage in any way, this legislation should actually be welcomed by men. The very fact that women workers are placed upon a basis of equal pay for corresponding work is in itself an advantage to men and an assurance that the wage level will be maintained. This is therefore a matter of just as great interest to the men who are in the ranks of our workers throughout Canada as it is in the case of the women. Nevertheless, there is a special reason why we all welcome this legislation. Mr. Chairman, our expert on this particular question has already registered the opinion of this group. I should like to say, Mr. Chairman, that this question of equal pay for equal work is something that has been at the masthead of the labour movement of North America, and perhaps of sections of the world where there is a labour movement, for a good many years. The slogan "equal pay for equal work" is all-inclusive. What we are doing now, of course, is establishing that principle in so far as federal employees are concerned.
When a bill such as this is passed in the country everybody outside immediately thinks that it is legislation that applies nationally. You get a lot of letters such as you receive on antidiscrimination, but it merely applies to federal employees.
The minister made it clear that he believed this bill affected some 73,000 female employees employed by the federal government. Of course, all legislation is as good as its administration and there are going to be administrative difficulties in this. There are one or two thoughts I should like to leave with the minister. First, I think the need for this legislation was proven by the job evaluation surveys made by most of the labour unions throughout North America during the past 15 years. Practically every industry of any size is now organized and has its research personnel. Part of that research personnel consists of job evaluation officers. During the surveys that have been taken over the past 15 years a need has been shown for this type of legislation. The statistics upon which that need is based have been gathered by most of the labour unions across the country.
I think the war proved that there were many sections of industry where women could be employed, but at the beginning of the war, as those of us who were in the house at that time can remember, in shipyards and in other industries where women were trained to take jobs it was the practice of the employer to try to hire them for 15 per cent, 20 per cent or 50 per cent lower wages. During the process of the war the unions did a pretty good job in levelling out in the aircraft industry, in shipyards and in other industries, this question of equal pay for equal work. There are many sectors

Female Employees Equal Pay in industry where women can replace men and, in some places, such as the aircraft industry, they can do a better job and a faster job.
The point I should like to make to the minister is this: the enforcement of the legislation is very important. Where there are unions or civil service organizations already set up they have determined the schedules, the rates of wages, and how they shall apply.
With respect to the principle of this legislation, I would assume that the court of referees or the referees would come into the picture only after the union or the civil service organization has a chance of examining any protest that may be made by way of a grievance after it has gone through the mechanics of the bargaining contracts or the civil service schedule of rates. Then the board of referees will come in. I would want to be careful about it and to know that we are not setting up a superbody that is going to displace the mechanics of collective bargaining in industry, and there is some under the federal government, or the rates and schedules that have been built up over the years and the practices that have been laid down by the civil service. I suggest that any appeal to the court of referees should be processed through either the collective bargaining organization or the civil service organization rather than through an individual. I do not think we want to start writing collective bargaining agreements on the floor of the house. This is one point the minister will have to keep in mind.
Instead of setting up a court of referees that is going to handle individual grievances arising from individuals we should see to it that that court of referees come into existence only through the due process of the collective bargaining organizations, or the civil service organizations. This is the point I wanted to make, Mr. Chairman, and I trust that when the bill comes in the position and the authority of the court of referees will be clarified, and especially when they come into action.

I should like to say a few words on this resolution having to do with equal pay for women before the bill is introduced. Mr. Chairman, like all other hon. members of this house, and I am sure the people of Canada, I am glad to see this resolution make its appearance. It deals with a subject which has been necessary for some time to be brought in as legislation. This is legislation which is desirable and long overdue.
As the Leader of the Opposition said this morning, and as other hon. members have implied, the appearance of this legislation is due very largely to the efforts of the hon. member for Hamilton West, and the many women's organizations across Canada which have been pressing for it for many years past.
As the Leader of the Opposition said, the hon. member for Hamilton West introduced a resolution in 1953 which was not debated, and in 1954 and 1955 when the resolution was debated. Many of us were extremely sorry to see that the government did not adopt that very sensible resolution of the hon. member at that time and bring in this legislation several years ago. It seems regrettable to me that it has been held up so long. This is a matter that has been discussed thoroughly by labour bodies for some time, and it seems to me there has been unnecessary delay in bringing in this very desirable legislation.

As was also indicated by the Leader of the Opposition, this is not only good legislation for women; it is also good legislation for men, because it protects their jobs. As one who has been connected with industry for some time, I know that in many industries, if it is found that a woman can perform a job as well as a man, the man will be displaced and a woman will be taken on in his place because she can be hired at a lower rate of pay. If it becomes necessary by law to pay women the same rate that is paid to men for doing a certain job, then of course the men who might formerly have been displaced will not be displaced in future, and this will be a protection for their jobs.
As has been said this morning, this legislation is in operation in five provinces, and I very much hope that it will soon be in operation in all of our ten provinces. I think this legislation will be an example to the other five provincial governments to bring in similar legislation as soon as possible. I also hope it will serve as an example to industry generally, and that equal pay will be afforded to women in the near future for jobs which they perform alongside of men.
The hon. member for Waterloo North said that the children of working mothers were very often neglected. Social workers report that generally this is not the case, and that the children of working mothers are frequently better looked after than are those of non-working mothers. I am wondering from what the hon. member said this morning if he is making a charge against the working mothers in his own riding of Waterloo North that they do not look after their children as well as mothers who do not work.

Mr. Chairman, like many other hon. members I am interested in this resolution practically, I suppose, because it seems perfectly obvious and reasonable that if a piece of work is done well the employer

Female Employees Equal Pay should not care very much by whom it is done and the remuneration for the doing of such work should be the same whether the person who does it is a man or a woman or even a child, despite the fact that it might take the child longer to do it. Please do not misunderstand me. I am not going to take the retrograde step of going back to child labour which it took so many hundreds of years to eliminate.
Philosophically, I suppose, I am interested in the bill because it is another step in the long struggle for the emancipation of womanhood. That is also too long a story to go into here.
I really rise to my feet for one purpose and that is to bring out an idea which I do not think has been brought out sufficiently strongly this morning although the minister, when he spoke, quite rightly paid tribute to the work of the hon. member for Hamilton West and the work of Miss Agnes Macphail, both of whom were advocates of legislation of this sort in this House of Commons. All honour to them and to others like them. I am quite sure that the efforts of Miss Macphail in particular-and I say this with due deference to the hon. member for Hamilton West, but Miss Macphail got an earlier start- certainly had a great influence upon the thinking of labour unions and farm people and most certainly upon the thinking of the hon. members of the political movement to which I belong.
We have, of course, some cases where discrimination of various kinds raises its ugly head even in this extremely advanced country, or so we call it, of ours. Fortunately it does not exist in the same degree as in some other countries. I remember watching some girls selecting oranges from a movable belt to pack them in boxes. The girls on one side of the wall had skin of one particular colour and those on the other side of the wall had skin of another colour. I asked the foreman what the wages were in each case and I discovered that the ratio was about 4 to 1 in favour of the girls of one particular complexion, of one particular ethnic group, amongst the people we saw working.
When the minister was speaking he used the words "the crystallization of public opinion". I was thinking perhaps more of the initiation of opinion amongst the public in regard to these things. It occurred to me that it is not always and indeed it is not often those people who are burdened with the responsibilities of government who lead in the fight for reforms of various kinds.
I am thinking, for instance, that when we talk about the emancipation of women we should be ashamed of ourselves that women

Female Employees Equal Pay received the vote at such a late date. My thinking takes me away back to the scenes and days of my boyhood when the suffragettes used to throw bricks through the glass windows of shops in London. You could perhaps call them fanatics if you like. They certainly were fanatical along that particular line but I suppose their fanaticism served a useful purpose. I think their attempts to gain independence occurring prior to the first great war certainly impressed the minds of the people during the war when women did come into their own in the matter of taking their place side by side with their men in the war factories of Great Britain.
The point I really want to make is this. I said it is not always those who are burdened with the responsibilities of government who are the cause of reform and I think that is perhaps one of the most valuable functions of an opposition. I am thinking of private members' resolutions such as those we had introduced in this house by the hon. member for Hamilton West. In this party we have an hon. member who has probably introduced more private resolutions than has any other individual, and I am thinking of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre. There is satisfaction in seeing certain ideas embodied in legislation. Ideas advanced by the hon. member have proved to be of benefit, as will this resolution, to the people of this country.
Legislation providing for the emancipation of women indicates the great need there is throughout the world for greater steps to be taken to see that women are given the franchise. I shall not attempt to give a list of those countries where the franchise is denied to women, but I do want to emphasize this idea of private members bringing forward resolutions which quite often are the basis for legislation some time in the future. Sometimes I find some fault with the impatience shown by my friends on the government side. They are quite often inclined to be impatient with resolutions moved by members of the opposition. That impatience to me is very childish. They take the attitude that they are the government, that they should run the country, that they should bring in any resolutions which are needed, that they represent the will of the majority. The practice is to toss out or to vote out any resolution moved by the opposition.
I am coming back to the minister's statement about the crystallization or I would say the initiation of public opinion in regard to any particular idea and which eventually finds itself incorporated in the form of a resolution which is of benefit, not only to those who are in opposition but to those who sit on the government side.


I know that I have at times wearied the house with a resolution in regard to federal aid for education. I remember one misguided Liberal friend-they are not all misguided -who characterized that resolution as being simply a move for political purposes, a deliberate attempt to deceive the public. That simply indicated the supreme ignorance as to one of the most important functions of the opposition.
That is the point I thought I would make in regard to this resolution. I do believe that members can perform a useful service to the country by bringing up such matters in this house. That is one of the things we were sent here for. We should bring up these matters so that they may become publicized, so that they may be discussed throughout the country, so that they may become popular. Then the government, which is always watching which way the water is flowing or, if I may use another simile, which always has its ears pretty close to the ground, decides that, as a majority of the public wants it, it will bring in a resolution to that effect and the thing becomes law.
I congratulate the government, I congratulate the minister, I congratulate those who initiated this idea. I am pleased it has been brought before us and I shall look forward with interest to seeing the terms of the bill.

It is not my intention to take any more than a minute or two to say a few words in support of this resolution. Equal pay for women for work identically equal to that done by men certainly should have the support of every member of this house. The resolution limits this, however, to federal works. The resolution reads:
To provide equal pay for female employees as compared with male employees of the same employer, for identical or substantially identical work in federal works, undertakings or businesses;
It seems rather ridiculous that a resolution has to be introduced in 1956 to establish the right of women to receive equal pay for equal work. By what right can employers say, "You get less pay for doing exactly the same work as a man, merely because you are a woman"? It is a relic of the dark ages. It is a shameful thing that this has lasted as long as it has in Canada. We are at last taking a belated and very short step towards establishing some elements of justice in this field. It is an unfortunate thing that the government of this country had not recognized this right earlier. I can remember
30, 1956
Female Employees Equal Pay during the war years asking ministers of labour to establish this right for the women when they were working in the factories and war plants and carrying on their task while men were away fighting and to recognize that the women who did such a splendid job should receive the same pay for the same work. That right was denied.
This bill moves towards the elimination of a piece of discrimination which should never exist. If a women did not do the same amount of work, I would say that perhaps she is not entitled to the same pay, but if she does the same work by what right has the employer to make more money out of her employment than out of the employment of a man? Out of such employment he makes so much profit for his organization and the company that he is directing and operating. I do not know why that should exist in Canada. We are pleased certainly to see at last this little bill coming forward and saying that in federal works at any rate the women who do identically equal work will receive equal pay. We have advocated that for years, and I have never heard one person give a legitimate reason why the women should not receive equal pay. This group has fought to remove this discrimination against women ever since the party was formed in 1934. We are glad to see them moving forward. The day is not far distant when organized labour will unite and demand of the governments in all parts of the country that this be universal and that when a woman does the work of a man she should receive equal pay.
I do not know why the government has sat in power for 20 years and has continued to receive the support of the people when it would allow this kind of thing. It is merely a sign that the people are not aware of the injustice, or those who should be speaking about this matter are not doing so. Perhaps the new organization of Canadian labour will take up this subject. Perhaps the fact that the national unions organized in Canada are united at this time is belatedly causing the government to move. At any rate, let us hasten this legislation through and let us wipe this injustice and discrimination against women off the books in Canada and establish a condition in this country to which we can all look with pride.

I have no objection to doing as my hon. friend has suggested. This bill will do four things. In the first place it will provide that the succession duties which are payable in respect of the estate of a deceased pensioner may be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund and then deducted by instalments out of the pension or allowance in order to avoid too great a burden upon the pensioner all at once, especially where the pensioner is a widow.
In the second place, there is a provision which is to permit the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police who were absorbed into the force from the province of British Columbia to count for pension purposes all of the time that could be counted for pension purposes under their pensions from that province. As my friend the hon. member for Kamloops is aware, when we took over the policing of the province of British Columbia we took over several members-there were about 15 that would be affected by this bill -who were absorbed into the mounted police. The purpose is to make sure that when they get their pensions they will derive benefit in them not only from the service that they have had in the Royal Canadian Mounted Police but also for service they had in the British Columbia police force.
This legislation therefore has nothing to do with the point about which my hon. friend spoke, namely increasing or changing any benefits in respect of the pensions of members


of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police generally. It is just to take care of accrued pensions of the members of the mounted police taken over from the province of British Columbia.
Then we have the same problem with regard to those members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police that were taken over from the province of Newfoundland when that province, which was then a colony, became part of confederation.
The fourth purpose of the bill is to provide for additional liability to the Royal Canadian Mounted Police pension fund resulting from general pay increases. In other words, if we increase the pay a larger amount must be paid into the fund correspondingly. This bill will provide the mechanics whereby that amount can be paid.
