speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 443, to amend the Supreme Court Act and the Criminal Code.
He said: Mr. Speaker, I think perhaps this bill is of sufficient importance that I should make some brief comments on the motion for second reading. The bill will try to avoid certain anomalies and to provide certain conveniences for the administration of the court in a general way. The four main purposes of the bill are as follows. First of all, there is a provision to establish the office of deputy registrar of the court, the intention being that either this new officer, namely the deputy registrar, or the registrar of the court himself will personally report the decisions of the supreme court. With the abolition of appeals to the privy council, now that the Supreme Court of Canada has become the court of last resort in this country, it becomes increasingly important, I think, that the highest possible standard of service should be given in respect of the reports of its decisions. We therefore feel that the editing of these reports, and particularly the preparation of the summaries and head notes and -we hope-the argument of counsel, should be undertaken by a senior officer of that court. After this new arrangement goes through we will have a senior officer look after it. Inasmuch as the registrar could not possibly do it and also look after his ordinary work the arrangement, as I have said, will be either that the registrar or the deputy registrar will do the work of the court registrar and the other of the two will do the reporting. In this regard we have been very fortunate in getting the services of Mr. Harvey who up until quite recently has been editor of the Ontario Law Reports and who I think, by
Supreme Court Act
general consent, is regarded as the most able law reporter in the Dominion of Canada today.
Second, we propose to increase from $2,000 to $10,000 the minimum amount that must be involved in a case appealable as of right to the Supreme Court of Canada. The present amount-that is the $2,000 limit-was fixed in the province of Quebec some years ago, in 1875, to be precise and for Ontario the amount of $1,000 was fixed in 1896. In 1920 the sum of $2,000 was made uniform in all of the provinces, and this amount has remained unchanged to the present day. That is to say, the amount that may be involved to entitle a litigant to appeal as of right to the court of last resort in Canada has been, and is at the present time, the same as it was in Quebec in 1875, in spite of the fact that the purchasing power of a dollar, whatever dispute there may have been as to the change in it in the last 10 years, is certainly very much less now than it was in 1875.
Now, this increase to $10,000 would reduce somewhat the number of cases that reach the Supreme Court of Canada as of right but, of course, leave to appeal may always be granted by the Supreme Court. Therefore, what we are dealing with here, inasmuch as all of the other cases can be handled on the basis of application for leave to appeal to make sure that there is some principle *of law involved, which should have the consideration of the Supreme Court- what we are really dealing with here are these cases in which there is only a question of fact which has already been passed upon by the trial court and by the appeal court of the province. I think in most of those cases it will be open to quite considerable doubt as to whether there is any purpose in having a further appellate court go over what is a pure question of fact and arrive at some different disposition from that which has been affirmed in both the trial court in which were involved the judge and jury, who have had the opportunity of hearing the evidence given by the witnesses and all of the advantage that that brings and in the provincial court of appeal.
The Supreme Court of Canada, of course, can be applied to for leave to appeal in any cases where that seems to be warranted. It is simply a question of their not having the appeal as of right in these cases we are now discussing.
Third, we propose to alter the procedure on appeal; that is the method by which a litigant who is appealing from the provincial court of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada launches an appeal in the Supreme Court. The normal method in the provincial

Supreme Court Act
courts is for an appellant to serve a notice of an appeal upon all of the opposite parties to the suit and then file that notice of appeal within the prescribed time in the court of appeal. Under the Supreme Court Act, however, the practice heretofore has been that no notice of appeal is served or filed. Instead the appellant must make an application to the court to have the security for appeal that he must give approved; and when the security is approved the appeal is deemed to be commenced notwithstanding the fact that the other parties to the case have received no other notice of it.
We think it is desirable to bring the appeal procedures in the Supreme Court of Canada into line with that which prevails in the provincial courts of appeal. The bill, therefore, will provide for the launching of the appeal to the supreme court by notice of appeal, by filing it with the registrar within the time prescribed by the act.
Fourthly, we propose to amend the Supreme Court Act and the Criminal Code with respect to the applications for leave to appeal in both civil and criminal cases. At the present time an application for leave to appeal in civil cases must be made to the court, but applications for leave to appeal in criminal cases are, under the Criminal Code, made to a single judge of the court. It is proposed that in all cases the application for leave to appeal should be made to the court but that the quorum on the hearing of the application would be three judges in both civil and criminal cases with the single exception that in capital cases the quorum would have to be five judges.
I think I should point out in that connection that the joint committee on capital punishment made a recommendation the other day that is somewhat different from this provision here, namely, the recommendation which would provide an appeal as of right to anyone who had been convicted in a capital case, and also other recommendations to the effect that the provinces, because it would be the provinces that have the responsibility for the administration of justice, should in such capital cases see that the accused was provided with competent counsel to defend him if he had no means of providing counsel himself.
I suppose there will be those who will say that we should give immediate effect to the recommendations of the joint committee. I am suggesting to the members, however, the present provision for these reasons. In connection with the report of the joint committee on capital punishment, on corporal punishment and on lotteries, there are a number of provisions which can only be implemented by those governments in Canada which, under

the British North America Act, are responsible for the administration of justice, namely the provincial governments. In the Fauteux report, which was tabled the other day, there are, it is true, quite a large number of provisions which can be implemented by the federal government, but there are a larger number which must be implemented either by the federal government and the provincial government acting together or which the provincial governments only can implement. That being so, we have felt that inasmuch as these various reports all deal with aspects of what, after all, is one entire problem, namely the administration of justice in the enforcement of criminal law, the least that we could do would be to confer with the provincial attorneys general who have the primary responsibility for the administration of justice, before we attempted to take any action within our own sphere of jurisdiction here to implement recommendations in which the interest of the provinces is at least as great as that of the federal government, if it is not greater. I say that because while we may enact these provisions, it is the provincial authorities that have to enforce them. As we all know, as I think it was stated in this chamber just this very day, no law is any better than its administration. Thus when we are dealing with a problem of this sort we should certainly confer with those who have the responsibility of that administration before we attempt to make any changes in it. Therefore I am recommending to my fellow members and to this house, sir, that in the present circumstances we adopt for the time being this provision that in capital cases the application for leave to appeal should be made to a quorum of five judges; and that this will stay in effect until such time as we can discuss with the provinces, for example, whether they are prepared to undertake this responsibility, which has been suggested, that they should provide counsel if necessary for the accused. We should also at least pay them the courtesy of getting their reaction to this idea of there being an appeal as of right to the supreme court, in which, if they are to undertake the cost of providing the counsel, they must have a considerable interest.
It is for that reason I recommend, as I have said, that we adopt this provision with regard to the quorum upon the understanding that we shall discuss this other matter with the provincial authorities. If a reasonable majority of them are agreeable to adopting this other provision and if we ourselves are advised, that this is a wise provision, we will bring in later amending legislation to provide for it.
There are one or two other minor matters which I do not think there is any purpose in

my mentioning at this time. These four provisions are the main items of the bill and I think we can go into the other details when the bill is in committee.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there are certain very grave reservations that we have with respect to this bill notwithstanding that in a number of respects it will effect a considerable improvement over the existing arrangements.
The most important ground of criticism as far as we in this party are concerned is that we regret exceedingly that the department has not seen fit to take the important and long overdue step of providing that in capital cases, that is mainly in cases of murder trials, there shall be an appeal to the supreme court as of right. We think that the time for such a provision is long overdue.
After all, as appears from the bill now before us, in civil cases up to the present time involving sums of only $2,000-when I say "only" I am referring there to the sense of comparing a sum of that nature with a man's life-in civil cases involving only $2,000 the appeal is as of right. It is true that the bill before us proposes to raise that limit or that floor, as it were, to $10,000, but I may say at once we are opposed to that. If it passes, then we are still going to have the fact that when a cash sum of $10,000 is in dispute you have an appeal as of right, but when a man's life is hanging in the balance you have to go and apply for leave to appeal. We consider that to be an entirely anomalous situation and one which runs counter to the concepts of justice which should prevail in this country.
The minister has said he is recommending the present proposal, that is that there should be an application for leave to appeal in capital cases to be heard by a quorum of five instead of by a single judge as in the past, but he is doing that instead of going all the way and enacting at once the provision that appeals will be heard as of right mainly on the ground that he feels the provinces should be consulted before the step we recommend is taken.
I might emphasize here that this step, namely making appeals on capital cases as of right, is recommended in the recent report of the special joint committee on capital and corporal punishment, as the minister himself pointed out. The reason the minister said he felt they should consult with the provinces was because the provinces would have to undertake certain expenses in connection with the hearing of appeals if they were allowed as a right and therefore the provinces should be consulted first.
Supreme Court Act
I suggest that that argument is insufficient on two grounds. In the first place it is not as though this were a new suggestion made for the first time and embodied anywhere for the first time in the report of this committee. This is a suggestion which has been before law enforcement officers for consideration for many years. Secondly, the argument that there might be some financial expense incurred by the provinces is one which I venture to say that no province would have the temerity to suggest publicly as a reason for arguing against the adoption of the suggestion.
That sort of argument, to my mind, is even worse than the situation which we find prevailing where, if you have $10,000 in dispute, you can appeal as of right whereas if your life is hanging in the balance you have to apply for leave to appeal.
When a man's life is placed in jeopardy as a result of a charge laid by the crown of whatever province it may be, then it behooves us and it behooves the provinces equally to see that that man has a proper defence and a fair trial; and if, as we recognize in the very fact that we have a supreme court and in the powers of appeal we give it, there are certain issues which are so important that they require to go before the Supreme Court of Canada and we require that court to hear the case as a court of last resort, then to my mind there can be no excuse for saying that this supreme issue, of whether or not a man shall lose his life as a result of our judicial process, shall not come before that court as of right and that we are going to wonder whether we should give the man the statutory right to go to that court because it might involve some expense to the law enforcement agencies of this country. That is an argument I cannot support for a moment. It is not an argument, I believe, that any province would advance publicly. It is just not an argument. It is a line of reasoning that does not stand up in the light of the issues which we are considering in this question.
The minister has said he considers that the matter should be left in abeyance until this report of the committee and all its implications can be discussed with the provinces. That means we are not going to have legislation until next year at the earliest. I point out to you, sir, that men are still being tried for murder in Canada and particularly now when the whole question of the retention or abolition of capital punishment is a question which is so greatly exercising the thoughts of our people it seems to me to be an untenable position for the Minister of Justice to take to say we are going to delay

Supreme Court Act
any longer in granting an appeal as of right to the Supreme Court of Canada in a capital case.
If there had been an appeal as of right the situation in the Coffin case would never have arisen. I have already expressed my very critical views in this house of the conduct of the minister and the results that developed there with respect to the manner in which that case was handled. As it was, because there was no appeal as a right, because there had to be an application made for leave to appeal and because of the way that matter was handled, there exist in the minds of millions of Canadians, I should imagine, very grave doubts as to the final outcome and the execution in that case. That whole messy, unfortunate and deplorable situation should not have arisen. I know the minister has been urged before that we adopt legislation granting appeals as of right.
I admit that this will be a substantial improvement if the bill carries, even if the amendment which we propose to move in committee is not accepted; but this legislation will still be a great improvement over the previous provision where such application came before one judge. However, I express the greatest regret that the minister has not seen fit to go the whole way and grant appeals as of right. I cannot refrain from expressing the gravest criticism against the grounds on which he has rested his case for his decision not to go that far.
The other main ground of our criticism of the bill is that it increases from $2,000 to $10,000 as the minimum sum which must be involved in civil litigation before there is an appeal as of right to the supreme court. I do not believe it is sound that appeals or the right of appeal should be governed by the financial amount in dispute. I recognize that in almost every province there is a division between the initial jurisdiction of the county court, on the one hand, and the supreme court or its equivalent depending upon the province, but that is only the initial hearing. Once a decision has been given, whether it be in the county or supreme court, as far as I am aware-I hope those who come from other provinces will correct me if I am wrong-there is the same right of appeal from the county court to the appeal court of the province as there is from the supreme court to the appeal court. That limitation or differentiation as to the original jurisdiction is of no application to the principle we are discussing here as to whether there should be a financial limit applicable in the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada.

The minister says that the limit of $2,000 was made uniform in 1920 and that there has been a change in the purchasing power of the dollar since that time. That argument is not sound in principle. If it were the minister would have to establish that the purchasing value of the dollar has declined five times, that in 1920 the dollar would purchase five times what it will today. That is a sorry admission to come from the government which has been in power I should think on a rough calculation at least two-thirds of that time. I do not think that any such argument can be maintained because it is not a sound principle on which to base the right of appeal.
If the purchasing power of the dollar should go up, will there be another amendment to lower the limit? Are we to vary the ceiling or the floor on the amount in dispute before there can be appeal as of right every time the cost of living index varies? As I say, I am not satisfied that it is sound in principle to have a financial limit in matters of this kind and I am absolutely opposed to raising it from $2,000 to $10,000. Two thousand dollars may be more important to a litigant, particularly one who is not blessed with many resources of his own, than $10,000 may be to another litigant. The principle of law involved in the $2,000 case may be as important if not more important, but because the amount in dispute happens to be $9,999 instead of $10,001, if this bill goes through there would have to be application for leave to appeal in the one case with appeal as of right in the other.
In this connection may I point out that when you interpose this obstacle of having to make application for leave to appeal you impose upon the litigant in a civil action or the accused in a criminal case an extra cost in addition to the cost of having his appeal heard. That is a reason additional to those I have advanced why appeals in criminal capital cases should be as of right.
I should like to revert to this subject of consideration for a moment and say that I feel there is an urgent necessity for further reform in our criminal law with respect to the providing of adequate facilities for the proper skilful and thorough defence of every one accused with a capital crime. I regret to say it must be confessed that there have been cases, certainly in the initial hearing, where an accused has been grossly prejudiced by an inadequate defence because of lack of funds. I know of one such case, and those with whom I have discussed this have told me that they have personal knowledge of similar cases.

I submit that so long as that situation exists we cannot disclaim responsibility in this parliament because criminal law is a matter of federal jurisdiction. Some of the responsibility must be shared by the provinces whose duty it is in the administration of justice to appoint counsel for accused who cannot afford to retain their own. I believe this matter requires the most careful and immediate consideration by the bar associations and law societies of the various provinces.
While we are undertaking a general study of the question of capital punishment, while we are considering this question of the right to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada in capital as well as other criminal cases, this other matter also requires to be considered immediately by the department with a view to bringing down at the next session-I doubt if there is time at this session-some amendment or improvement to our law so that it can never be charged against us in Canada that a person accused of a capital crime has Suffered because of inadequate defence.

speechtext:
Yes, Mr. Speaker, I think that probably this matter is one that does require detailed discussion in committee, and I shall defer my further remarks under this heading until that time.
The third criticism we have to make of the bill is that it follows what we regard as an unsound legislative principle in that it incorporates into one amending bill provisions relating to two entirely separate statutes. We have raised objections to this same procedure being followed on other occasions. Whilst I realize there may perhaps be some room for difference of opinion as to whether it is a sound legislative practice, I regret to see it being adopted by the department which should set the pattern for legislative excellence, namely the Department of Justice. This bill is entitled "An act to amend the Supreme Court Act and the Criminal Code", which makes it obvious that it is amending two separate statutes. This means that from the day this bill is given royal assent and is proclaimed, those seeking amendments are going to have to look in two different places to see what is the effect of one bill. If this practice were enlarged upon and carried forward into the future I think our statutes, between the periodic revisions that occur, between the times when there is a complete revision and revised statutes, would become a hodgepodge in which it would be even more difficult for lawyers, let alone laymen, to find amendments than now.
The minister may say there are only two acts and the amendments deal with the same general subject, appeals to the Supreme Court of Canada. That is so, but if you are applying the principle, then why apply it to three, four, five, or six bills, and so you can go on? Either the principle is sound or unsound. We regard it as unsound, and we intend at the appropriate stage to move accordingly that the bill be divided.
In these remarks I have made I have expressed in perhaps strong terms criticisms of the bill. I do so because I do not think there is any more important field of legislation than this, and we here have real regret that the bill does not grapple with the problem and solve it at once, in fields where we believe solutions are urgently called for. Nevertheless I must in fairness say that we believe that the provision with regard to the appointment of the deputy registrar is sound; that the simplifications of the procedure with regard to appeals to the supreme court is, generally speaking, desirable and
[The Acting Speaker (Mr. Applewhaite) .1
sound; and the provision for a quorum of five in capital cases, whilst it does not go as far as it should and is to that extent subject to severe criticism, is nevertheless as far as it goes, a real improvement.
The one thing for which I cannot find any justification and about which I cannot find one kind thing to say is the raising of the floor for appeals in criminal cases as of right from $2,000 to $10,000. Because the bill is not capable of amendment to bring about the things we would want at this stage but only in committee, and because as far as it does go it is an improvement, we intend, notwithstanding the quite severe strictures we have made about it, to support it on second reading and then make real efforts to improve it in committee.

speechtext:
I shall be very brief. I wish to support what was said by the hon. member for Kamloops as far as this bill is concerned. It is an improvement, with the exception, as the hon. member pointed out, of the increase from $2,000 to $10,000, for leave to appeal cases as of right. Like the hon. member, I can see no justification for that, because after all these appeals are not entirely a matter of monetary consideration; they are a matter of privilege, and I do not think the amount of money involved should have any consideration whatsoever.
As the hon. member pointed out, it is much easier for some people to appeal because of a $10,000 consideration than it is for many others to appeal because of consideration of the $2,000. I think it should be thrown wide open, and the monetary limit should be abolished entirely. If it is not going to be abolished, then it should be left at the $2,000 mark. I think this section of the bill is untimely and unnecessary.
Referring briefly to capital cases, I think the quorum of five is sound, but like the hon. member for Kamloops I dislike intensely the thought that a man appealing a murder conviction is given less consideration than somebody suing for $10,000. A $10,000 tag on a man's head is entirely unjustified. I should like to see appeals made possible as of right in capital cases. I only hope that if the minister is not willing to do so now he will take the report of the committee on capital punishment and talk it over as quickly as possible with the attorneys general and law enforcement officers of the provinces, so the necessary legislation can be brought in to provide these people with an appeal as of right.
I hope he will introduce such a bill as soon as he can at the next session and have it passed, because it is an unfortunate thing

that a person condemned to death cannot have an appeal as of right but has to make application for leave to appeal. It is an unfortunate thing and, as I said before, a man's life has a very low price tag on it when compared with the $2,000 or $10,000 limit in civil cases.

Well, Mr. Chairman, I think it would be very difficult to say in general terms what would be the cost of the different cases unless one knew what factors were involved; for example, how much it would cost to provide transcripts of the evidence which they will already have had before for the provincial court of appeal. But the point which the hon. member for Fort William raises is quite important, and presents an angle of this matter that I think perhaps has been overlooked by those who have taken part in the discussion until now.
If some plaintiff in a very clear-cut case where the facts cannot be challenged, is able to secure a judgment in a trial court and then is taken, we will say by an insurance company, to the provincial court of appeal and goes through the expense of that court,

and then is subjected to a further appeal to the supreme court he may, if he has not a long enough purse to keep up this process of briefing his own counsel, be put in rather an embarrassing position. That is another side of this same question.
What this present clause provides is that where there is, in cases between $2,000 and $10,000, a successful litigant who has got a judgment of the trial court and has maintained that judgment in the court of appeal, he cannot be taken further into the supreme court in a case which, for the most part, involves only questions of fact. For if some principle of law were involved, as the hon. member for Kamloops mentioned, then it is inconceivable to me, and I am sure to him, too, that the supreme court or indeed the court of appeal of the province itself, upon application for leave to appeal, would not grant leave to appeal if there were some principle of law involved that needed to be settled.
It may be that the step from $2,000 to $10,000 is too great a step to take at one time, but I do think the limitation which was imposed in the first instance in Quebec in 1875 does not make sense in 1956 in the whole of Canada. And it is not only upon the question of the purchasing power of the dollar, though it is true I did mention that as one of the circumstances. It also has to do with the nature of the cause of action. For example, there will be a good many automobile collision cases which arise under present circumstances, having regard to the value of the cars involved and the like, which will easily run up above $2,000; they may run to $3,000, $4,000, $5,000, and $6,000, having regard to all the people who may be injured. Now, if it is a clear question of fact; if that has been threshed out in the trial court and an appeal has been taken to the appeal court of the province, and it has been gone over again there, is any real purpose served by one of the parties, the party against whom the judgment has gone, being able to take this question of fact to the Supreme Court of Canada and have it gone all over again by the judges of that court, who already have a very heavy burden of litigation at the present time?
I do not think the matter of whether it should be $10,000 or some lower amount is one upon which the government would want to take too firm a stand, but I am certain that it is not fair either to the litigants on the one hand or to the supreme court on the other that we should retain in 1956 this money limitation which was first put into effect in this country in 1875.

speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, we now come to the two clauses dealing with the amendments to the Criminal Code involving the question of the right to appeal to the supreme court in criminal cases, and so far as we are concerned here the main subject of consideration is capital cases. As I said earlier, we feel that in cases where the penalty is death the accused should have the absolute right to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada for final adjudication, instead, of having to apply for leave to appeal.
I do not think I have very much more to say, except to point out I do not feel the argument that provincial attorneys general would be faced with extra costs is really one that can be seriously advanced or seriously maintained where a man's life is at stake. The only argument I can see for justification for the present proposal is if the minister were to tell me that when the application for leave is heard-if the amendment carries, it being then subject to be heard by five judges -they are in effect disposing of the appeal itself. On the face of it that is an attractive argument. For that reason I think it is so much better to have five judges than to have one, as was the case formerly; but it is not quite that simple.
What is being argued in the application for leave is really and properly of a much more restricted and technical nature than the appeal proper. If leave is applied for, it being the duty of counsel for the crown who would be opposing the application for leave to see that the points argued on that application are not extended beyond the proper legal limits, then I do not think it is a safe argument for us to accept that the court is in effect hearing the appeal itself when it hears the application for leave to appeal. I think this is so important that every safeguard all the way through, including this most important one of an appeal to the court of highest resort, be granted to an accused person on a capital charge, that I propose to move an amendment to this section which I shall read. I move:
That section 19 of the bill be deleted and the following substituted therefor:

Subsection 1 of section 597 of the Criminal Code is repealed and the following substituted therefor:
"(1) A person who is convicted of any indictable offence whose conviction is affirmed by the court of appeal may appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada
(a)	in any case where the conviction is for an offence punishable by death;
(b)	in all other cases;
(i)	on any question of law on which a judge of the court of appeal dissents;
(ii)	on any question of law, if leave to appeal is granted by the Supreme Court of Canada within 21 days after the judgment appealed from is pronounced or within such extended time as the Supreme Court of Canada or a judge thereof may, for special reasons, allow."
If, sir, you will compare that proposed amendment with section 597 (1) of the Criminal Code as it now stands you will see that the effect of it is this. Subsection (a) as it presently appears in the code now becomes subsection (b) (1) of this amendment, and the proposed subclause (b) of section 19 of the bill appears as subclause (b) (2) of the amendment. In effect all that is done is to insert a new subclause providing that in capital offences leave shall be as a right.

I want to reinforce the argument which has been advanced by the hon. member for Kamloops. We have here a proposal that in offences where the punishment may be death, there shall be a right to appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada. I believe that recommendation has been placed before the house in another manner. It is something which has been approved of by lawyers in all parts of Canada, and I think there has been a recommendation by the Canadian Bar Association to this effect.
This amendment should commend itself to the sentiments of hon. members generally. A ceiling of $10,000 is being placed on appeals in civil matters, but even when considered on a mercenary basis the right to appeal is automatic when the amount involved is over $10,000. Are we to say that a life is not worth $10,000? As I say, this amendment should appeal to hon. members generally.
There is something repugnant in the idea that a man or woman sentenced to death is precluded from an appeal as of right. There is a procedure followed in my province which might be adopted by the Supreme Court of Canada, and I think the same is true of most other provinces. There is an appeal as of right on matters of law in both criminal and civil cases. Then when there is a question of both fact and law, or of fact, the appeal is by leave. The practice with our provincial court is for the court to hear the application for leave to appeal, which usully involves a complete review of the facts and the law. If that application is granted almost invariably the appeal is granted at the same time. That is possibly one way in which this matter could be dealt with.
I repeat that this amendment should commend itself to the committee. It covers something which probably will be law in the near

future. The mere fact that it might possibly involve provincial governments in some expense is no reason that I can think of why this matter should be deferred in order that the provinces may be consulted. If it is right, it should become law whether the provinces approve or not; if it is not right, the approval of the provinces has nothing to do with it. It is a matter of morality; it is a matter of justice, as well as being a matter of law. I repeat that this is an amendment which should commend itself to the committee.

Mr. Chairman, I submit that the hon. member for Kamloops has rendered a service in the study he has given to this bill and the recommendations he has made to the committee. A matter of this kind has to be handled by one learned in the law. I listened to the hon. member very carefully when he spoke on second reading, and I agree with everything he said. If there is one thing to which the Department of Justice should be paying particular attention it is the question of whether a person involved in a capital case is getting justice.
We have had more than one example where a man is picked up and finds himself faced with a capital charge and the difficulty of getting defence counsel. I think all that should be dispelled. I submit that the amendment moved by the hon. member for Kamloops is absolutely in order. When a man's life is at stake an appeal should be automatic.
When you consider the application to appeal and the cost that is involved, the average person who is affected, in the circumstances that the bill describes, is just not able to handle the cost. I think the time has now arrived when the Department of Justice, regardless of how the provinces may look at it, should lay it down as a principle of justice that, as far as we are concerned, it is not going to be a matter of money in order to get into the Supreme Court of Canada, that the right of appeal should be automatic, and a thorough examination should be made by the five judges, as we have it now-and that is an improvement.
I do not think there should be any question. There are enough lawyers in this house, and I believe every one of them, if they were to express a private opinion and there were no political implications, would say without any hesitation that the amendment suggested should be adopted. There should not be any quibbling about it.
Perhaps it is a matter of an oversight on the part of the drafters of the bill, and they did not analyse it in the way in which it has been analysed by the hon. member for Kamloops. I do not want to repeat anything he

speechtext:
I am afraid that the remarks I made at a previous stage of this bill on this particular subject matter have not had much effect upon those who have taken part in the present debate, and for that reason I should like to attempt to elucidate a little more effectively than I did before just what our position is in this matter.
There certainly is not any question of an oversight. We in the Department of Justice began the over-all revision of the Canadian Criminal Code, which had not been consolidated for over 60 years, as the first step toward what might be regarded as an examination, if not an overhaul, of the administration of criminal justice in this country. We then followed that up by the appointment of the Fauteux committee and then the two commissions under Chief Justice McRuer and then the joint committee of both houses of parliament. All of these committees and commissions have been dealing with separate branches of the criminal law. We now have the Fauteux report and the three reports of the joint committee of parliament. We hope this fall to have the reports from Chief Justice McRuer. We shall then have a review of all of those portions of the criminal law and of penal reform that have not already been considered in the revision of the Criminal Code which was passed by this parliament.
Having regard to the fact that the enactment of the criminal law is the responsibility of this parliament of Canada, and that the administration of justice and the enforcement of the law is exclusively a provincial right and responsibility-and it is a responsibility to which every one of the provinces attaches a great deal of importance for very obvious reasons-I am sure the provinces would not want the federal government stepping in and interfering with their enforcement of the law and their administration of justice. In those circumstances it is no oversight that we have decided that the whole field that has been examined by the Fauteux commission and by the two royal commissions under Chief Justice McRuer and by the joint committee of this house and of the Senate, should be, as a matter of the most primitive form of courtesy, if for no other reason, discussed with

those who are responsible for the enforcement of the criminal law, before we undertake to bring in any legislation in this house which will have to be enforced by them.
If we make any allowance at all for common sense, surely we must realize that the people who are right on the firing line of the enforcement of justice must have gained from that experience over the whole history of our country some insight as to what the law should be, that is the substantive law; and also an excellent idea as to what are workable procedural changes.
Therefore, even if we were not trying to maintain something which is of the very essence of good criminal law in this country, those good relations between the federal parliament which enacts the law on the one hand and the provincial legislature and government which enforces the law on the other, but if we were only to regard the matter of bringing before parliament wise provisions of law, we should certainly want to have a discussion of these reports that we have obtained from the various commissions and the joint committee of the two houses of parliament with the provincial attorneys general and law enforcement officers. To what end? To the end that we shall thereby be able to bring in a much wiser law than would otherwise in my judgment be available. We need not be so taken up with our own conceits that we should think that, having little or no experience with the administration of the criminal law, we can reach judgments that cannot be a little better if we consult with those who have extensive actual experience.
In this particular matter that is under discussion, I do not know how the government could have gone any further toward meeting the viewpoints that have been expressed here this afternoon than by putting into effect at once the provision which the hon. member for Kamloops himself is frank enough to admit is a great improvement; that is, that application for leave to appeal would have to be made to a quorum of five, which is a majority of the whole Supreme Court of Canada. Unless we are going to say that this quorum cannot be depended upon to adopt a fair attitude toward the applications made to it, and therefore we have to give an appeal as of right because the quorum will not deal with such applications satisfactorily-unless we take that view, which I think would be quite unwarranted, then in this interim we have a very good and very workable provision to take care of the very points that have been disturbing the minds of those who have taken part in this immediate debate.
Supreme Court Act
I have said-and if there is any doubt about it I want to make it clear now-that our consultation with the provincial authorities over the whole field covered by the Fauteux report, by the two McRuer commissions and by the three reports of the joint committees of parliament will be to the end of securing a criminal law more workable in all its aspects. If, after having had that discussion, it appears that it is feasible and workable, and that it will work out in practice as we think it might be good in theory to have this appeal as of right to the Supreme Court of Canada, then, as I have indicated in the clearest possible terms, so far as the policy of this government is concerned, there is nothing in our minds at the present time that would stand in the way of bringing in that reform.
But surely, even if we did not think we would have a wiser grasp of this whole problem after talking to the people who have had all the responsibility of enforcing it, even if we only thought that as a matter of courtesy between the two levels of government we would get a better enforcement of our law if we observed some of the civil amenities as between the two levels of government, on that ground alone the course we are presenting would be a wise one. May I remind the hon. members who have spoken that no law is any better than its enforcement. So if we are going to have a better substantive law, which will work better, we have to carry along the judgments of those people who are going to enforce that law. Therefore on all these counts the procedure we recommend to the house is the one which I think should be adopted, and for that reason I must oppose the motion.

speechtext: I said that the criminal law enactments we put through in this house have to be administered by another level of government; that the criminal law, like all other law, is, so far as the ordinary citizen is concerned, no better than its administration, and that in my judgment for that reason it is a wise and essential move that in these matters affecting another level of government we should consult those who are going to enforce the law, not with the view that they should have any kind of control over our judgment but at least that we should hear from them as well as from commissions, committees and so on before we bring this law into parliament for enactment.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Did not a committee of parliament sit for two years and hear from the provincial representatives? What more does the minister want?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: I shall answer that question right away.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: And it brought in a recommendation after having heard from the provincial representatives who were invited there to make their recommendations.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: My hon. friend asked a question and I shall be glad to answer it. We want to discuss with the provincial administrators of justice recommendations that were the product not only of the evidence given by the provincial people, but of a large mass of other evidence as well.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
Certainly; and the committee heard them and brought in a recommendation that in a capital case an appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada be granted as of right. That is not a matter of procedure. It is a matter of principle, a matter of whether or not this parliament believes that

people accused of murder should have the right to go to the highest court in the land. When it comes to working out how that will be done, making provision as to the time at which transcripts and factums will be transmitted and who is to be responsible for the cost of the appeal if the accused does not prefer to retain his own counsel, that is a matter of procedure and should most certainly be discussed.
But we are only asking here that there be a decision on the principle after the due consideration that has already been given to the matter and after the opportunity that has been given already to the provincial representatives to be heard. I believe the minister has a case with respect to the other matters of enforcement of law, penal reform on which the Fauteux commission has reported and so on. These are cases where practically every decision taken is going to have to be administered by the provinces, the jail provisions and so on.
But that is not so here. This is a decision on principle on which we are asking for action now after, as I said, the provincial representatives have already been heard from. Men are now being charged and tried for murder. I do not say that is so at this very moment, but there are murder cases pending, and men's lives are depending on them. There is a case for justification and a basis for delay in respect of the other matters. They are serious matters, but after all it is not a vital matter to put a man in the wrong sort of jail or administer the wrong sort of penal reform, things which may be changed after the recommendations of the Fauteux commission and others are considered. But you cannot change your mind about taking a man's life by hanging, and the question of whether or not he has the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada may determine whether or not his life is taken by hanging. We have heard from the provincial representatives, and it is a matter of principle upon which parliament is entitled and I think is under a duty to decide at this moment.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: May I ask my hon. friend a question before he takes his seat? Is his argument to the effect that the application for leave to appeal cannot safely be entrusted to a quorum of five Supreme Court of Canada justices?

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
It is not my argument at all. The minister again is seeking to camouflage the question. What I am saying is that you are placing obstacles in the way of a man accused of murder having access to the Supreme Court of Canada if you make him

come forward and obtain leave to appeal, because you are imposing upon him an additional burden of expense and difficulty.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext: Before you put the question, may I say that I am in the same position as the minister. I cannot recall all that was said. However, I should think it will probably be found that the reason they did not say that is that they were not asked, and the reason they were not asked is that the committee did not regard it as a matter where it was vital to obtain a decision or because they regarded it as a matter of principle on which we should make up our minds and upon which the provincial representatives were perfectly free to express an opinion if they wished. The fact that they did not express an opinion is significant, in my mind, to show that they were not asked because the committee regarded it as a matter for decision here.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I suggest to the minister that where hearings have been held in the lower courts at the provincial level, frequently local or provincial feeling is quite strong. It seems to me that the right of appeal to the Supreme Court of Canada should be available to every Canadian in order that he could be removed from any provincial atmosphere that might affect the situation.
Of course, as the minister says, a committee of five judges sits and studies whether or not the right of appeal should be granted. However, in the case of capital offences it seems to me we are moving in the wrong direction if we place any obstacles in the way of Canadian citizens that may deny them the right to appeal to the very highest court in the land. It seems to me that right should be undeniable and should be known to everyone.
I deplore the trend here. It seems to me that the move to increase the floor from $2,000 to $10,000 and the whole trend is to try to lighten the work of the Supreme Court of
Supreme Court Act
Canada. I think the judges of the court are well paid. They are paid to do a job, and surely the matter of justice should not be a matter of cost.

subtopic: AMENDMENT TO PROVIDE FOR CHANGES IN CONNECTION WITH APPEALS, ETC.
speechtext:
I think I made my position on this matter perfectly clear, Mr. Chairman, when I spoke on second reading. I think the minister should not only take into consideration the evidence that was taken in the committee in this regard, but should remember this fact. He was talking about co-operation and the relationship between the federal government and the provincial governments. I want to remind him that this is not a matter of social amenities. It is a matter of whether or not some of these cases which are now pending are going to result in the death of a man or woman while the minister is observing the social amenities as between the Department of Justice of this government and the departments of justice in the provincial governments.
This is a matter of life and death, or at least it could easily be so. Surely to goodness nobody in this country has a better right to appeal as of right than a person who is convicted of murder and who could be hanged. I want the minister to think about this matter. As was pointed out earlier, it is a matter of principle. Regulations and so on surely could be worked out, having regard to the responsibilities of the federal government and the responsibilities of the provincial governments so far as money and costs are concerned. Those matters can be worked out later. But this is a matter of principle about which I feel very strongly. I think that a man should certainly have the right to appeal without any worries in that regard. Let the Minister of Justice and the attorneys general of the provinces work out their various little problems later.

In 1955 the Fort Smith plant was extended and improved by the installation of a fourth generating unit and erection of a fuel oil storage tank, the total cost of which was approximately $48,000. speechtext: Mr. Chairman, this bill was considered at some length in the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines; and therefore the opposition do not feel that there is any necessity to take a great deal of time on it today. However, there were one or two amendments made in the committee and it would be helpful if the parliamentary assistant would explain these.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, before explaining the two amendments which were brought in by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, I wish to acquaint hon. members with the fact that the minutes of the proceedings of the committee were placed in the mail boxes of hon. members this afternoon, but there are some 25 copies on the Clerk's table available to hon. members

Canada Shipping Act
at the present time. This bill was considered at great length by the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines and two amendments were made.
The amendments will be found in Votes and Proceedings of Friday, July 20. The first amendment has to do with clause 9 of the bill, which deals with section 119 of the act. As hon. members will recall, this clause deals with certificates of service granted to mariners who have demonstrated their ability to operate their vessels through actual experience but who because of lack of basic education are unable to pass the ordinary examination for a certificate of competency. Under the present section a mariner applying for a certificate of service is required to supply evidence of his service and pass a simple examination consisting of an eye test, knowledge of the fundamentals of the rules of the road and in the case of home trade vessels a knowledge of one-flag international signals.
There has always been an understandable reluctance on the part of many mariners, particularly older men, to appear before examiners, and many of them had not obtained their certificates before the expiration of the time limit. I should say that the section dealing with these certificates of service provides that the mariner shall have served as master of a home trade inland or minor waters vessel for a period of 12 months within a period of 10 years starting with 1948. The bill provided that this limit be extended indefinitely, and some objection was raised in committee to the fact that while a mariner might have acquired experience in waters such as the Newfoundland coastal waters or in the St. Lawrence he would have no experience, say on the west coast.
Therefore an amendment was moved in committee to the effect that the minister would be empowered to limit a certificate of service to waters described in that certificate. This was done by an amendment to subparagraph (c) of clause 9 amending section 119 of the Canada Shipping Act, which adds at the end of the subclause (c) the words "within the limits prescribed by the minister and specified in the certificate".
Following this first amendment to subclause 1, the wording in subclause 2 had to be changed somewhat. I should first explain that the previous subsection 2 said that the holder of a certificate for a vessel under 150 tons could on application be entitled to surrender his formal certificate and have this certificate endorsed so as to be good for ships of up to 350 tons. Since we are now limiting the application of these certificates to certain waters we could not have this provision in the new subclause 2,
[Mr. Langlols (Gaspe).l
because it might not be in the interest of some holders of present certificates to obtain new certificates, which would be endorsed for ships of higher tonnage but limited to certain waters. Therefore it is for this reason, as hon. members will notice, that new subclause 2 as amended by the committee does not contain the provision that "the holder is entitled upon surrender thereof to be granted a certificate under subsection 1 for those waters."
That deals with the first amendment. The second amendment is a very simple one and it has to do with clause 25 of the bill. This clause was amended in order to further clarify the wording used in the first part of the clause. The amended clause reads as follows:
(1)	The international convention for the prevention of pollution of the sea by oil, 1954, set out in the fourteenth schedule (hereinafter called the convention), is approved.
(2)	The governor in council may make regulations-
Then (a), (b) and (c) follow. A period was added after "approved" in the original text, and the clause was divided into two subclauses, one dealing with the approval of the convention and the second giving power to the governor in council to make regulations. As I said, this is only a matter of further clarification of the wording of the clause.

On clause 2-Exemption from registry.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Clause 2 makes a provision that ships from 10 to 15-ton registry shall no longer be required to effect registration under this act. Hitherto the exemption has been for ships under ten tons. This is only one of several changes made in the Canada Shipping Act by these amendments, which have the effect of lowering standards. I doubt very much the wisdom of doing that in connection with this act.
The Canada Shipping Act has been the basis of our marine law for many years. Before that we depended upon the merchant shipping act of the United Kingdom. The provisions, by and large, have stood the test of time. Yet here we are making a change so that it will be no longer necessary for ships from 10 to 15 tons to be registered. They will be thrown into the category of the smaller ships which are licensed and which number about 120,000- these, of course, are the small motor boats running around the Ottawa river, the Rideau canal and the various lakes in Canada- about 120,000 small boats licensed under the Canada Shipping Act, as distinguished from ships that are registered. From now on

ships from 10 to 15 tons may come into that category. It will not be necessary to register them.
The parliamentary assistant told us in the committee that there are about 17,000 ships registered in Canada, as distinct from those that are licensed, and of that number 3,354 are in the category of from 10 to 15 tons, there being 857 on the west coast and 2,497 in the rest of Canada.
I am afraid this change is one that is unwise and really not necessary. We were told in the committee that it was done in order to cut out red tape. I suppose we should all be in favour of doing away with red tape in governmental activities, but this practice of registering ships has been a very important factor in our whole shipping picture. Apparently no shipping organization asked for the change. For example, neither the merchants' exchange in Vancouver nor any of the other organizations there interested in shipping asked for this change. Apparently it was requested by different individuals. 1 am wondering whether a good many of them are not owners of pleasure boats who did not want to be bothered registering their ships which might be from 10 to 15 tons. However, from now on it is not going to be necessary to register them, and in my opinion that breaks down the formalities of registration which have been in existence for so long.
The parliamentary assistant took the position in the committee that the department is not very particular about this amendment, and that if the committee saw lit to recommend going back to the old law, that is, that only ships under 10 tons should be exempt, there would be no objection from the department. I hope that since the sittings of the committee the department has had time to consider this matter further, and I would ask the parliamentary assistant now whether it would not be possible to leave the provision as it was before; as it is under the law at the present time. The present section 8 reads as follows:
8. Ships not exceeding ten tons register tonnage employed solely in navigation on the lakes, rivers or coasts of Canada and pleasure yachts not exceeding ten tons register tonnage wherever employed or operated are exempted from registry under this act.
I suggest that we would be wise to continue that provision rather than make the change contained in clause 2 of the bill.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
As I explained to the committee when the bill was considered there, this amendment is to provide that ships are exempted from the requirement to be registered if their net tonnage does not exceed 15 tons. Here we are dealing
Canada Shipping Act
with net tonnage. The law as it stands puts that limit at 10 tons and we are now asking that it be raised to 15 tons. I wish to remind hon. members that owners of ships below 15 tons net tonnage will still have the privilege of registration if they wish to do so. Otherwise they must take out a licence, which involves a much simpler method. I also wish to repeat what I said in the committee, to the effect that this has nothing to do whatsoever with building standards and inspection requirements. The ships that are registered or licensed will be subject to the same requirements that apply to all other ships covered by the inspection regulations.
I also wish to add that in adopting the new limit we are following the same practice that has been adopted in the United States and in the United Kingdom. All we are doing is to relieve the owners of these small craft from the trouble of going through the complicated procedure of registration when we think that registration achieves no practical purpose. As the hon. member for Vancouver-Quadra put it, and I think I used the same expression in the committee, all we want to do is to cut red tape and cut down on formalities when we are of the opinion that formalities and red tape achieve no practical purpose.
Moreover, in the committee I also gave figures indicating that even with the present exemption for ships below 10 tons net registered tonnage our list of shipping shows that well over 1,000 ship owners with ships below 10 tons have found it convenient to register them, and they are in fact registered and appear in our shipping list. Raising the exemption from 10 tons to 15 tons does not necessarily mean that all owners of ships between 10 tons and 15 tons will take advantage of the new limitation, but they will be at liberty to register or license their ships as they wish.
A while ago the figure of 3,000 ships was mentioned as being the number of ships which will be affected by the change, but it must be said that this is the number of ships between 10 and 15 tons net tonnage which are actually registered. The amendment of the provisions of the present section raising the limitation to 15 tons does not mean that these ships will automatically cease to be on the registry. They can be withdrawn from the registry only on application of the owner, and unless the owner takes that action the ships will continue to be registered.
As far as the attitude of the department is concerned, I expressed it in the committee when I stated that the department was not

Canada Shipping Act unduly insisting for this amendment, but I must say that we have since considered the remarks made in the committee and we have not been convinced that the amendment proposed in the bill should not be carried. We must bear in mind that the registry of these small ships involves a lot of work in the department, and if we can cut down that work when we think it is possible to do so without affecting the requirements of the department as far as inspection is concerned, I think we should do so. For these reasons I believe the proposed clause should remain as it is. As I said a moment ago, all we are seeking to do is cut down on red tape and formalities which achieve no practical purpose.

Clause 25 is the clause which deals with the international convention for the prevention of the pollution of the sea by oil, and that convention is included as a schedule to the bill. As the parliamentary assistant knows, section 495a does two things. In the first place it gives power to the governor in council to make regulations for carrying out the international convention which aims at preventing pollution of the sea by oil. In the second place it gives power to the governor in council to make regulations to prevent the pollution by oil from ships of any inland, minor or other waters of Canada. There are two distinct powers contained in section 495a.
I take it that it will be some time before the international convention becomes effective, and it is unlikely that there will be many cases under the convention off the coasts of Canada outside territorial waters. As far as the west coast is concerned, as soon as publicity appeared concerning the prevention of pollution by oil there were favourable comments in all the Vancouver newspapers. There we have had trouble for quite a number of years-I am sure the Minister of Fisheries will agree with me-caused by the pollution of the waters off our shores by oil, sometimes from ships and sometimes from


refineries. I guess the worst case of pollution in Vancouver harbour was caused by a refinery.
I urge upon the parliamentary assistant that prompt action be taken to have regulations drawn up and put into effect dealing with the pollution of our own waters. I should like to bring this matter to the attention of the parliamentary assistant. Every year there is a big death toll by drowning on the great lakes. speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I did not rise on section 1 because there was no necessity to do so, but I do want to say that the committee made a very comprehensive and complete study of this bill with the assistance of the parliamentary assistant and his officials. I think all the members of the committee recognize the competence with which the parliamentary assistant handled his end of the discussion. We are also indebted for the very clear-cut and informative answers we received to questions placed before the officials on various sections of the bill.
On the basis of our study of the bill in committee, and recognizing this as a technical subject in which we have to rely to a great extent on the experience and ability of the officials, this group supports this bill as a move in the right direction and something that will end up to the general advantage of the people of Canada.

We were particularly pleased by the introduction of section 27, which provides for the licensing of the operators of small boats on inland, minor and other waters. A number of the members of this group have noticed the increasing number of small boats on our various waters, and as in the case of the increasing traffic on our highways there is no question but that the time has arrived to have some regulation with respect to the licensing of boats and the licensing of operators.
We realize that legislation of this type is not going to be introduced suddenly and be functioning perfectly within a short time. We were therefore very pleased to learn that it is the intention of the department to implement the legislation gradually as the result of co-operation with launch clubs, yacht clubs and other persons who are interested in navigation and the operation of boats. We were also interested to learn that the department is doing something to educate the public, in the terms of the legislation, as to the necessity of licensing boats, and I presume they will do the same with respect to the licensing of operators. I think the small pamphlet that has been issued by the department is very excellent indeed. I think it is a very sound and democratic procedure to seek the co-operation of the people in the administration of legislation of this type, and I believe the department is to be complimented for adopting that approach to this situation.
During the discussion on this section there were some interesting remarks made concerning the question of life preservers. That subject was in the minds of a great many members of the committee as the result of some extremely unfortunate accidents that occurred in recent weeks. During the discussion some members of the committee cited their various personal experiences concerning life preservers that had been sold to people in various parts of Canada. I for one was very surprised to find that you can buy a life preserver marked "government approved". I personally thought it meant that the preserver was approved by the Department of Transport, but the committee learned it simply meant in some cases that it was approved by the provincial department of health as being new material, as in the case of a bed mattress. But that is not of much concern for your health if you happen to drown when you are wearing the preserver.
In that connection we in this group think the department should do everything possible to inform the public of the situation with respect to life preservers, and ask

that they only purchase life preservers which have the approval of the Department of Transport if they wish to be safe when they are on the water.
In that respect we urge a continuing educational program as far as the operators of boats and the public generally are concerned. We think the department should do everything it can to co-operate with the manufacturers. I am sure that when the public and manufacturers and all concerned understand the situation it will not be too long before the public in its own interest and the manufacturers in their interest will co-operate with the Department of Transport for the greater safety of those who travel on our beautiful lakes, rivers and other bodies of water.

Am I to take it there will be no regulations in effect before the remainder of this boating season; is that right?
Canada Shipping Act

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.

There may be a few

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext:
Am I to understand that
although it is two years since the conference, the United Kingdom is the only country which has become a party to the convention?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.

subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
speechtext: Is there any prospect of the ten countries, including the five which have this gross tonnage of 500,000 tons in tanker capacity, becoming parties to the convention in the near future?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.

We hope so. We are
informed that the convention is being considered by the governments of a number of these countries.

When the required number of
countries have become parties to the convention, it will take a further period of 12 months before the convention comes into effect?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING REGISTRATION, CERTIFICATES, ETC.
