speechtext:
The house resumed, from Tuesday, July 3, consideration in committee of Bill No. 418, to amend the Income Tax Act-Mr. Harris- Mr. Applewhaite in the chair.
Income Tax Act
On clause 1-

Mr. Chairman, in a sense I am fishing outside the territorial waters of second reading. I began to speak just before the motion for second reading was carried, and by arrangement it was agreed that I and the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, I believe, could carry on with a few general remarks on the first item.
I had been drawing attention to a number of examples of changes in the Income Tax Act which might very well have been considered by the banking and commerce committee had the bill been referred to that committee, where some of the ideas which originate in the house-and I think some very good ideas originate in the house with respect to income tax-might have been put forward and discussed and perhaps received more serious consideration than they do under the method now employed in making up the budget and the amendments to the Income Tax Act. The amendments in the bill are largely technical, and in so far as they are not they carry out the decisions of the minister as disclosed in the budget address.
I had indicated one weakness of our income tax legislation in comparison with others countries, namely that not enough consideration is given to the parents of children. Not enough deduction of taxable income is allowed for those who are raising children. Certainly we do not do as well in Canada as is the case in other countries. I had cited the example of Great Britain.
I now refer to one oddity of the act. If a man is fortunate enough to have a child toward the end of the year he is immediately entitled to family allowance with respect to that child, and the deduction from his taxable income which he is entitled to receive goes down from the $400 for a child not receiving the family allowance to $150 for a child who is getting the family allowance with the odd result that although only one instalment of family allowance may be paid for that child, that is, the December payment, the father loses $250 by way of deduction from income and gains only one small payment of $5 per month by allowance. That is a rather Irish way of putting it but that is the effect of the regulations as they are because there is a great difference between the amount allowed as a deduction and the tax payment received in the case of a child in receipt of family allowance and one which is not. It makes a difference of perhaps $45 to a parent in that particular circumstance.

Income Tax Act
Another type of exemption which it seems to me could well be considered by the committee is the encouraging type of exemption which would permit the father of a family or a householder who wants to see his child educated in a good school to deduct the school taxes which he pays to another governmental authority. I have raised this point before and I raise it again. It seems to me it is one that deserves serious consideration, particularly in the light of the responsibilities which municipalities have now and which they will have to load on the home owner. It would not result in the loss to the treasury of a great deal of revenue and it would be easing the lot of the parents of children who, as I say, are not as well dealt with under our income tax law as they are in some other countries.
Another sort of exemption which would be good and which would be an encouragement to the enterprise of our people is an exemption which would allow a family to deduct from taxable income the amount paid for medical and health insurance. Certainly it is a problem which is receiving consideration. The problem of health insurance is one that receives consideration from all levels of government, and it is a big issue. But it seems to me it would be an encouragement to those who are prepaying their medical and hospital costs if they were allowed to deduct those payments from their taxable incomes. It would not be difficult to work out an arrangement by which medical expenses, which are now deductible if they are more than 3 per cent of income, or prepayments on insurance of this kind could be deducted, depending on whichever was the larger.
Another item with which I want to deal I can leave until clause 3 is reached, because it relates to the change in the exemptions allowed to the teaching clergy. However, there is one other item with which I wish to deal and that is the position of the selfemployed. I wish to say a few words again about that issue, because it has again escaped the attention of the minister in his revision of the numerous sections which deal with approved pension plans. I see that they are now called registered pension plans. There are quite a number of provisions in the act dealing with them, but there is no relief for the self-employed. There is no correction of the injustice which has been pointed out time and time again in this house, and which has been the subject of representations to this government for at least ten years. I refer to the injustice which exists as between the position of those who are employed and are on payrolls and that of those who are working for themselves, with respect to the

pension fund savings which they are permitted to make and to deduct from their taxable incomes.
I want to bring to the attention of the committee the people who are involved in this issue. They are the self-employed, the people who are in the professions and those who are working for themselves, such as the farmers and so on. They are set out in the very excellent table of statistics which the Minister of National Revenue produces each year. I refer to "Taxation Statistics" for 1955. At page 9 each profession and occupation is listed separately, beginning with the medical doctors and surgeons. There were 10,000 of those who paid income tax in Canada in the year ended 1953, which is the last year for which figures are given. They are not all the doctors, because there are upwards of 14,000 in the country, but 10,000 of them are in the income brackets and they paid on an average of $11,000 of income each in the year 1953.
Their case is, I think, quite a special one, and it was presented to the government not so long ago in a brief of the Canadian Medical Association in which the argument I think is stated very clearly and very well. They say that over the past ten years repeated representations have been made by the medical association separately and jointly with other professional associations to the effect that self-employed taxpayers should be entitled to make provision for their own retirement. Such encouragement could best be demonstrated by permitting income tax deferment on personal purchases of annuities and other retirement funds in the same manner that now applies to approved pension plans.
The committee well know that the approved pension plans are available only to people who are employed, who are on payrolls. They can set aside up to $1,500 of their own earnings and their employers can put in an equivalent amount, making a total of $3,000 with respect to current purchase of pension rights for the future. That is all deducted from the income on which the employee and employer pay taxes in the current year. The fact is that an employed man, when he is at the height of his earning ability, is able to put aside money on which he has not been taxed for a pension which will be paid to him when he has retired and when he will be taxed at a much lower rate. The case for the medical profession seems to me to be particularly good.
Not only the medical profession; every other profession.
Income Tax Act

Mr. Chairman, I am not quite sure that I shall be making the same speech now that I would have made when we were on second reading, when the hon. member for St. Paul's and I agreed to let that pass. A lot of water has gone under the bridge since then. However, I have one or two matters that I should like to bring to the attention of the committee and of the minister on the consideration of this bill, which involves, as somebody suggested, a variety of amendments to the Income Tax Act.
I think perhaps clause 1 of this particular bill has some rather interesting material in it. I note, for example, this change which extends the phrase that requires the inclusion of the value of board and lodging to any other benefits of any kind whatsoever. Perhaps when we get into the detailed discussion of the bill the minister might be prepared to give us some reason for what appears to be a rather tightly drawn part of the act. Also in clause 1 is mentioned for the first time in the act, so far as I know, the matter of a supplementary benefit plan. I suppose that is one of the most important and in some ways interesting features of the Income Tax Act amendments this year, and certainly it is one that will be of great interest to the trade union movement across the country.
I would like to tell the minister that I have been having some discussions of this clause, pro and con, with one of my colleagues, the hon. member for Cape Breton South, and I have been rather inclined to defend the clause and say that it appeared to me to be a fairly satisfactory and fair arrangement. However, I should like to warn the minister that when we come to clause 19 of the bill he may have to do some explaining for the benefit of my colleague from Cape Breton South, because in the course of our private conversation he said to me-and I am going to quote him for the minister's benefit now-that he thought this description of the supplementary benefit plan was "wrapped in mystery, and like the language of Biblical parables was subject to as endless a variety of interpretations which later will be clarified by regulations written behind the scenes and which we will never see."
I thought at the outset of my remarks I should serve notice on the Minister of Finance that when we come to clause 19 he will have to give some particular clarification of it before the hon. member for Cape Breton South and myself are in complete agreement as to the meaning of this clause.
There are one or two points in this act that I have an interest in discussing, apart from the particular reference I have made so far to clause 1. One of them is the fact

that in the province of British Columbia, and perhaps in other parts of the country as well, we have an increasing number of organizations which are setting out to provide housing for senior citizens. In this regard I should like to supplement the plea that I know has been made by the hon. member for Okanagan Boundary in respect of some rethinking of the definition of what constitutes a charitable organization in this connection. Such an organization has been getting under way in the Alberni valley where I make my home, known as the Alberni valley memorial home society, which is set up as a community organization with participation by various local service clubs, trade unions, and other organizations of that kind, which are making contributions to this project. I have had sent to me a copy of a letter signed by the director of the legal branch and addressed to the secretary treasurer of this organization, which says:
After careful consideration we have come to the conclusion that Alberni valley memorial home society does not qualify as a charitable organization within the meaning of the Income Tax Act and donations to it are not allowable deductions under the provisions of section 27 (1) (a) of the act.
Well, apparently that is the position that has been taken by the legal branch of the Department of National Revenue; therefore it leaves open to members who are interested in this matter only the recourse of suggesting to the Minister of Finance that consideration should be given to an appropriate amendment to section 27 (1) (a).
There is one other matter, Mr. Chairman, that I should like to touch upon briefly. It has been brought to my attention a number of times, and I believe it has been touched upon by some other members of the house. I refer to the problems that arise in respect of the financing of the education of university students by the students and their families. I am not going to deal with this at any great length at this time, but I do feel there would be a great deal of merit in considering a change in the allowable exemptions of these people under the act for students at recognized institutes of higher learning. There should be allowed to them at least in addition to the basic $1,000 exemption the amounts they are required to pay in university fees. I feel, Mr. Chairman, that this would be a very beneficial change for our young people, who would find it easier to finance themselves or for their families to finance them in respect of their university education.
There is one other matter, Mr. Chairman, and this with me is not a new subject; it is a subject I have taken up during the last two sessions, and both times the minister has told me "no". However, I am going to persist in bringing this matter forward as long

as I am here and able to do so, until I feel some progress is made concerning what I have described as an injustice applied to those whose incomes are derived from wages and salaries in respect to deductions which are allowable for the expenses incurred in making a living.
I notice that in the Canada Gazette, part 1 of the July 21 issue, there is contained information bulletin No. 10 issued by the taxation division of the Department of National Revenue, from which it would appear, so far as this campaign which I and others, and certainly the trade union movement, have been conducting that perhaps we are going backward instead of forward.
While this information bulletin certainly does not change the existing law, it appears to be an indication that the Department of National Revenue is placing greater emphasis upon collecting every last allowable benefit that working people may have been receiving, and is making sure that employers do not allow employees any possible benefits in the way of free board or accommodation or transportation and so on even though they may have to travel a great distance from their homes in the course of earning their living. In one place it says:
However, employees who are hired lor the purpose ol filling a specific job away from home are not regarded as travelling "in the course of their employment". They are not on travel status for their employer but are in the same position under the act as employees who have to leave their homes and go afield to get work.
I do not agree that this is always necessarily the case. I have drawn the attention of the minister before to the type of problem that exists on the British Columbia coast, where there is something more than the matter of employees having to go to jobs away from home. In this case they may have to travel back and forth several times during the year because of summer shut-downs for fire seasons or winter shut-downs because of snow.
Under circumstances like those it seems to me there is a need, in our logging industry and possibly in other industries where this business of travelling expense is something that is necessarily incurred while an employee is making his living, for reconsideration. As I mentioned before, the same situation applies in respect to any allowable deduction for tradesmen in regard to tools or special clothes. If these things are going to be allowed to farmers and fishermen and in the course of business expenses to corporations and individual businesses, there is no reason why under reasonable circumstances there should not be some provision whereby people on
Income Tax Act
wages and salaries should not have the same sort of provision as this which applies in other connections.
While I am not too optimistic that the minister is going to get up and announce that he is prepared to move an amendment to the present bill, I feel there is an injustice under the present act, and it is certainly one which I intend to pursue with the minister as long as I have an opportunity of doing so.
As I say, Mr. Chairman, I shall defer any further remarks particularly with respect to the matter of the supplementary employment benefit plan until we get further into the details of the bill. These two or three points I wanted to raise prior to the committee stage, and I am very glad to have had the opportunity of discussing them tonight.

Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of questions I would like to direct to the minister on clause 1. In the first place the term "registered pension" appears throughout the bill to have taken the place of the words "approved superannuation". I would like the minister to explain why the change was made and what necessitated it. My second question is this. What type of benefit has the department in mind when it uses the phrase "of any kind whatsoever"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, concerning the first question the change of the wording to "registered pension" is to overcome the misunderstanding which I think has arisen over the use of the word "approved" in the present act. We do not approve pension plans as such. All that the Department of National Revenue does is to register pension plans whereunder the employer may be entitled to deduct certain payments made into the fund for income tax purposes. On the other hand, the use of the word "approved" would indicate that we had in some manner indicated approval of the plan itself, and we are trying to avoid that in what we are doing here.
With respect to the other question, we have in mind other forms of benefits that might be derived in the normal course of employment other than board and lodging. I think the hon. lady will understand, because she is well acquainted even with the law, that there is a rule that provides that when you use such words as "board and lodging and such other benefits" you are confining yourself nevertheless to board and lodging and some similar benefits, whereas there might be a benefit in connection with the employment quite apart from board and lodging which ought to be taxed, and that is the provision which we are making here.

Income Tax Act

Well, Mr. Chairman, I am concerned as usual with the advantageous position in which certain corporations and their employees are placed in comparison with self-employed persons. I am presuming that the minister it talking about such things as golf club memberships and so on.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, not quite that, although that might be it. An example would be the free use of motor cars and things of that kind which are taxed; some similar benefits of that nature.

Let us take the cost or service club fees. If a corporation is large enough it may pay the fees of as many of its employees as can qualify for membership in as many service clubs as happen to be in that particular district. These men who are working for a large corporation are deemed to be carrying out the service of their company, and quite rightly so; because undoubtedly they would not of their own volition belong to these clubs which are strictly on a classification basis. However, a self-employed person who likewise belonged to a service club for precisely the same reason an employee of a large corporation belongs to it is not permitted the deduction of those fees.
In my estimation that is not right. What is approved for one should be approved for the other. You may say, truly enough, that the individual who works for a corporation receives no personal advantage and I agree; and you might also say that the individual who works for himself does receive some personal advantage. The individual who works for himself may have some personal advantage; nevertheless he loses a great deal.
The same is true of the operation of a motor vehicle. A person may use an automobile registered in the name of an unincorporated company 99 per cent for company business, but the law says that if he does not possess another motor car he is deemed to use that car 25 per cent for personal use. Where a corporation makes a motor car available to an employee for his own use that employee has nothing whatsoever added to his salary for the advantage he gains from the use of that car, and the company is permitted to charge as a deduction the cost of operation and depreciation.
Those are the three things which come immediately to mind, but I know there are many others. There are dues for golf clubs, dues for service clubs and the cost of operating motor vehicles. I know from personal experience that the self-employed person is at a considerable disadvantage as compared with the person employed by a corporation.
fMr. Harris.!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Beginning at the last and working backward, where an employee of a corporation is allowed the use of a motor vehicle, that is added to his income for taxation purposes. It may well be true that in some cases the hon. member may know of the zealous Department of National Revenue not being able to find it, but in fact it is being done at the present time.
With respect to fees for service clubs, memberships and matters of that kind, it has always been thought that those would be an expense of the business concerned but they are not added to the income of employees, as the hon. member has indicated, in the case of corporations. I would suggest that the amendment before the committee at the present time may permit that to be done.
That does not give any advantage to the self-employed person who has all these expenses added to his personal income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There would be no disadvantage, because if you allow it as an expense to the corporation and charge it as income to the employee, there is no discrimination against the self-employed.

How can the minister account for the wholesale resignations from service clubs of persons who were members as representatives of their respective businesses, but who found the fees were added to their incomes for taxation purposes?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think the service clubs will maintain their present membership, because most members really feel it is an advantage both to themselves and to the community to belong to such clubs.

I was hoping the minister would comment on one point brought out by the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, that is the matter of donations to housing or cooperative bodies which are being set up for the purpose of providing low rental accommodation for older citizens. Such donations are not allowed as deductions for income tax purposes. Would the minister comment as to why this is not being done, and if there is not some way these bodies can get around the present act?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, I appreciate the remarks of the hon. gentleman, in particular the subject which he has brought to my attention. The real difficulty here is that to all outward purposes these companies which negotiate loans or arrangements with Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation to build tenements or homes for older people have on the face of it a profit motive. I think everyone realizes that there is no profit, at any rate not in the present, although there may be in

the distant future if in due course Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation are paid off. We would then have a building on which there was little or no debt, and at that point presumably profit would enter into the picture to the benefit of those persons who constitute the corporation.
On the other hand I am free to confess that if there were not such a possibility of profit we could very well consider that this might be held to be a charitable donation and therefore exempt under the act. All I can say at the moment is that I have been considering the point and will continue to do so. If some of the doubts which I now have can be overcome perhaps I may be able to say something about it.

This clause contains the words "of any kind whatsoever" and it seems to me that we are entering a really dangerous field. Somewhere along the line somebody is going to have to put a price tag on these services. For instance quite often the people living in logging camps are supplied with free wood and free light from the power plant, as well as other services. Somebody is going to have to put a price on those services. It seems to me that the thing is wide open, and it should be spelled out more firmly than it is.
What about firemen and policemen who wear uniforms which are usually purchased as a group? Is it intended to cover that by the phrase "of any kind whatsoever"?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No. Firemen and policemen and the like are not charged income tax on the value of their uniforms, and it is not intended to do so.

I was quite interested in the remarks of the hon. member for St. Paul's with respect to professional men, and making contributions to pension funds deductible. I submit that the self-employed person should have the same benefit as the person employed by others, but there is one particular group which I think deserves special consideration, and I refer to the medical profession. When I speak of the medical profession I am not including dentists. It is well known that some medical men make high incomes, but some do not. Generally those in the lower brackets are the hardest worked. Many of them work 18 hours a day to make the incomes they do.
I realize that in the large cities it is sometimes difficult to get a doctor after hours, as it were, but that is not so in the smaller communities. Doctors there work late at night, and when a doctor is sure the case is an emergency he will go out in the middle of
Income Tax Act
the night. I know from actual experience that many doctors work 18 hours a day and are on call 24 hours a day. It seems to me that if any concession is to be made, this group of professional men should receive special consideration.
Included in professional men we have lawyers. Personally I like lawyers as individuals, but it seems to me they are the one group of professional men that have a terrific advantage. They never have to work after hours, except those who are members of parliament and take their duties so seriously that they are here some Fridays and some Mondays. They may work after hours, but if they do it is by desire, because nobody is going to die through not having a lawyer. The rates of pay received by most professional men are as high, and a great deal higher in many cases. I am particularly thinking of the legal rates of pay. That seems to me almost a cartel or a combine; I do not know the exact word for it. However, the fee for the time involved is very great; often it is a percentage of the business.
Medical men get a certain fee; they are obliged by their oath to work at any time of the day or night, and they do. It seems to me that they, above all other professional groups-and I have no objection to all the other professional groups having this concession-should be entitled to this concession first, and then let it be spread out.
When I started to speak, I said I did not include the dentists in the medical profession. I like dentists as much as lawyers, as individuals; but it is a common practice today following extractions, if there is any bleeding or complication and you do succeed in locating your dentist, for him to say, "Call your doctor." That is a common practice throughout Canada today. I like to see them all happy but let us start with the medical profession first.

While the legal brethren are recovering their breath from the effects of the remarks of the hon. member for Timiska-ming, I should like to come back for just a minute to the question reintroduced by the hon. member for The Battlefords.
From what the minister says, I think that he would agree as regards the people who are contributing to the projects that we are discussing for providing housing, their gifts at the local level to get the project started are free-will gifts. Therefore there is a case for them to be regarded as charitable donations. I was wondering if the societies were to include a clause in their charters which would make it very clear that there

Income Tax Act
was to be no profit, a clause that would require that any surplus that might accumulate at a later time would be reinvested in improvements or expansions of that particular project, whether that might simplify the question of having the contributors to those organizations qualify on the charitable donations.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: May I point out that I thought we had passed through the general discussion, and that we were now confining ourselves to the actual clauses before us. However, just to answer my hon. friend's question, that is one of several ways that has occurred to us to consider the matter; but my hon. friend, I think, can take it from me that we are considering all the alternatives to see whether there is some plan that will meet the case. If I might say so, I would rather not discuss it further, because we should like to get on with the clauses.

I must come back to this question again. I am not quite satisfied yet. I am thinking now of the passes, for instance, that are granted to railway employees and employees of various companies in the transportation business, including T.C.A. and C.P.A. Surely we are leaving this too wide open. I should like the minister to say something on this and clear the matter up for me. I am not referring to members of parliament, because they come under the Railway Act and it is not passes that they or members of the Senate have, but it is other people who have passes. It would seem to me that they would be required possibly to say, "We had so many passes that were worth so much."

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I hope the hon. member will not put ideas into my head. I have no intention of taxing the value of free passes on the railways available for railway employees. If I did that I would feel that I should have to tax the free passes of members of parliament as well. So in those circumstances I am sure my hon. friend would let it go at that.

I should like to, but it was pointed out several times in the committee that any words that are said on the floor of the house or in committee have no bearing on the interpretation of the act. That being the case, it seems to me that it is too broad when it says "any kind whatsoever". Though the minister might give an undertaking here, I do not think, from my experience and from what I was told very plainly by one of the ministers, that means a thing. It is the interpretation of the act. I do not feel satisfied in that regard. I think the act is fully spelled out there.
[Mr. Barnett.!

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It is not, and that is why we are trying to extend it. There are some quite obvious things, such as the hon. member for Hamilton West has mentioned, which ought to be taxed; but there are those such as my hon. friend has mentioned that will not be. If it should happen that, using this broad clause, we get into a field where hon. members feel we should not be, this would be the place to attend to it; but under the present circumstances I can only suggest to the hon. member that there are benefits on which people ought to pay, and that is the purpose of the particular amendment.

As I understand it the act as it now stands reads "board, lodging and other benefits". I wish the minister could explain a little of what difficulties the department has run into in a reasonable interpretation of what are "other benefits", because this matter in a way is related to some of the other things I have been discussing.
The hon. member for Cariboo, I think quite rightly, has pointed out that in the outlying districts where facilities are provided by companies in the logging and mining business and occupations of that kind, there are certain things on which the hon. member mentioned putting a value. One of the concerns I have is that some of these companies may use this legislation to put on an arbitrary dollar value and start charging their employees or making deductions for things which by custom over a long period of years in the type of industry to which I have been referring have been provided as perhaps an inducement to people to go out to the more isolated and pioneering parts of the country.
"Of any kind whatsoever" is very broad. Whilst the minister says if this creates a difficulty he will be glad to consider it, nevertheless it might be much easier to consider the implications now before it becomes law than to wait till it has to come back here as the result of people crying about various injustices, and perhaps wait for the accumulation of quite a volume of them before anything is done about it. I wish the minister could give us some information as to why this change is deemed to be necessary.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
I have given one example
which I think is a good one, and that is the use of motor cars. There is no real provision in the act whereby we can assess for the use of motor cars except under a clause such as that which we are now placing before the committee. I think my hon. friend would agree with me that where an employee of a company is allowed a free motor car, or there is some arrangement made whereby he gets an advantage which you and I do not because

we have to pay for our motor ear, he should be taxed for it. A very strict construction of the words as they are now, "board, lodging and other benefits" may not include that because the words "other benefits" may relate directly to board and lodging and would not extend to cover motor cars. The purpose of the amendment is to take care of that type of thing. I do not suppose we will go to the limit at all that my hon. friend has suggested, but there are far more obvious advantages of a greater value that go to people and which ought to be taxed.

On the basis of the experience accumulated by the Department of National Revenue would there not be some advantage in adding a specific category? Would it not be enough for present purposes to add a suitable phrase to cover the question of transportation facilities? If other instances occur of real abuse of this provision then they could be added on the basis of experience, instead of creating a situation where someone in the field may get a wrong idea as to just how that should be interpreted.

In reply to various questions as to what it is the minister has in mind that he is seeking to achieve by the inclusion of the words "of any kind whatsoever" he has several times given one example, namely some benefit in relation to the use of a motor car. If there are other benefits that are within the contemplation of the government in introducing this measure then I think the committee should be told, but if only one has come to light and is in the mind of the minister now then it seems to me he has not made out a case for introducing wide words such as "of any kind whatsoever". If it is simply a matter of reaching motor car benefits, why should that not be spelled out specifically in the clause?
I think the discussion tonight must indicate very clearly that there are many hon. members who approach the amendment with a good deal of apprehension, because no one sitting here tonight can fully conceive what may arise some time and what may be included within these very broad words that we are being asked to include in the section. The words of the present section have been there for some years. The Department of National Revenue has had a good deal of experience with them, and I think we should be told tonight what are the specific benefits that are thought now not to be within the scope of the taxing provision, which ought to be; and we should be told the full list of them. Then we can judge every one of them on its merits.
If we are told of others it may be that hon. members will not think they are the
Income Tax Act
sort of benefits that ought to be included within the scope of taxable income. So far we have heard of only one example, and I say to the minister that if it is the only case that has arisen in the experience of the department the proper way to deal with that case is by a specific amendment, and not by including words of completely unlimited effect. One cannot imagine broader words than those, "of any kind whatsoever", and I think the reluctance indicated in the discussion thus far on the part of hon. members to include words of such broad effect is a very understandable reaction, when we are given only one example of what they might be applied to.

To follow that up, I think it has become the practice of the Department of National Revenue to interpret the act strictly as it is worded. If these words, "of any kind whatsoever", are included, what alternative are they going to have to taxing everything that can possibly be included, even uniforms of firemen, policemen and every other kind of item? More than once, and particularly in the estimates committee this year when considering the estimates of the Department of National Revenue, the department has pointed out how its hands are tied by the wording of the act. They say they have no alternative but to follow the wording of the act. It appears to me that they are not going to be given much alternative.

Mr. Chairman, there is one point that crops up at this time. I presume the minister is aware that employees of the C.N.R., for instance, are normally allowed about 10 per cent of their gross earnings for away from home expenses. I have had experience in helping fill out income tax returns for men on the C.N.R., and as long as the returns were sworn to they had no difficulty in having their away from home expenses deducted from their gross earnings, provided their expenses did not exceed 10 per cent. I am wondering how this regulation will affect that practice, which has already been adopted and more or less tacitly acknowledged by the department.
One thing that comes to mind as I look at the act is who gets it in the neck every time there is an amendment to the Income Tax Act. It is the workingman, and this is just another case where the workingman is going to be further punished by another change in the act. The hon. member for Timiskaming spoke of professional people. I happen to be a lawyer myself, but I have no sympathy at all for the way professional men may be treated under the Income Tax Act.

Income Tax Act
Who is the man who has to suffer by reason of our income tax laws? It is the workingman. When he goes on a vacation he is not in the same position as the professional man. He cannot offer the excuse that he is going to attend a convention and therefore claim his expenses as a deduction. I see that professional people are now allowed two conventions a year instead of one. The workingman is not allowed any conventions or any vacation expenses. Every time we turn around we find amendments being made which further cripple and hurt the workingmen of Canada. I think it is time we had another look at the situation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
My hon. friend has not taken time to look at the act or he would not have spoken as he has. There is a special provision in the Income Tax Act for the employees of the C.N.R. and other transportation companies to whom he has referred, and this clause does not refer to them at all.
To answer the hon. member for Eglinton, I do not suppose I could make a case on motor cars without also making a case on a number of other things, but it does seem that in a very short time we have turned from wanting to have this imposed as a tax on people to not wanting it. The hon. member for Hamilton West thought we should use this provision for the purpose of charging income tax on certain benefits that were obtained, and now my hon. friend seems to think we should not.
In fairness I think I should say that the hon. member for Hamilton West was seeking to terminate the discrimination which exists in practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: And the way to do that is to charge income tax on the benefits received by the employee. Now, there have been cases-	.
Will the minister permit a question at that point?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Certainly.
Does the minister not consider that the present section is broad enough to permit the inclusion within taxable income of that kind of benefit without any amendment?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No; that is the point of the amendment. It does not. It refers to "board, lodging and other benefits" and that means other similar benefits.
Does the minister not recognize that this clause will affect the provision regarding transportation company employees?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: There is no conflict. May I say that where there is a specific clause dealing with the costs of persons engaged in transportation, the law is in that section and not in a general section such as this. There have been cases where companies have paid the insurance premiums of their executives, have sought to have those as deductions and have objected to them being charged as income to the executives. There have been cases where they have supplied free furniture, free refrigerators, free things of that kind. These all ought to be added as income to the person receiving them.
May I point out that I know many cases where the insurance premium paid on the life of an executive has been charged back to that executive as income.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I am glad to know that.
And some of these other things that you mentioned.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: My hon. friend will join with me in hoping that this will cover the particular case.
It is covered now in this particular instance, or at least the Department of National Revenue has claimed it is covered.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: That may well be.

Has there been a determination on that point? With all respect, it would seem to me that the present language is broad enough to include a benefit of the kind referred to by the minister, namely, the payment of an insurance premium on the life of an executive by his employing corporation.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, there have been cases in which this wording "board, lodging and other benefits" has been brought into question as to whether it is broad enough to cover what we are talking about. That is why we are amending it.

Has the Department of
National Revenue ever had a case before the appeal board in this actual type of situation where the appeal board has ruled in favour of the taxpayer and said that the amount was not chargeable to a taxpayer's income?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Chairman. We have had a case in which contributions were made to a non-approved pension plan and when it got before the income tax appeal board it was suggested that perhaps these words were broad enough to cover it.
Is that not a different matter? That is a contribution to a pension plan.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: But it was in connection with the employee, not the employer.

With respect, Mr. Chairman, I think the situation referred to by the minister does not support what he was saying earlier as to the necessity for an amendment to include such examples as the payment of premiums on a life insurance policy for an executive. Can the minister point to a decision of the exchequer court or of the supreme court where it has been held that the language of the present section is not broad enough to include payment of an insurance premium in a situation of that kind?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No, Mr. Chairman, I cannot show a case where the income tax appeal board in fact held that these words did not cover the broad benefits concerned. But I can produce a case in which doubt was thrown upon it, and that is the reason for the amendment.

Although the hon. member for Eglinton protested, Mr. Chairman, I must myself register a protest against the minister's misinterpretation of my words. I am sure the minister himself knows that I was not attempting in any way to impose additional taxation upon any individual. If the individual is required by his employer to do certain things and to take certain benefits, wherein he has no choice so long as he maintains his employment with that employer, then you have a situation where his hands are more or less tied, and I do not think he should suffer thereby. Not only from what I have said tonight but from what I have said on previous occasions on various aspects of general taxation I am sure the minister knows that what I object to very strenuously is the discrimination against the self-employed and the small businessman who has an unincorporated business.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Shall clause 1 carry?

No, Mr. Chairman. I wish to come back to that matter, but first there is one other subject I wish to mention. In this clause and in a number of other clauses of the present act the minister proposes to substitute the words "registered pension" for the present expression "approved superannuation". He has drawn attention to some difficulties in connection with the word "approved" and has said that the Department of National Revenue really does not give approval. He is proposing to substitute the word "registered", and he says that the 67509-427J
Income Tax Act
department at the present time registers these plans. In the light of my own experience I am just wondering whether that is a very apt expression. Are any of these plans open to public view, or does the same secrecy attach to them as attaches to the return of the taxpayer?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The same secrecy attaches to them. It is not intended that there should be a central registry of plans. But in seeking to obtain tax deduction the employer must register the plan in order to get the deduction.

Then, Mr. Chairman, I think the word "registered" is a most inept word to use. Surely the word "registration" is one that connotes the filing of certain things in a public office, a place of deposit, where a number is attached to each document, and the time of registration is noted. In the public office, in an ordinary case, these documents are all available to view. But surely all that is done here, if the word "approved" is too strong, is to file. They are simply filed there. But surely registration implies something different from the operation that is carried out at the present time, and "registration" surely is not an expression that ought to be introduced here at all.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: For a long time we sought to find the appropriate word. It should be borne in mind that the plan is in fact presented for consideration, independent of the tax return that may be made at a given time. That is to say, an employer seeking to set up a pension plan would be obliged to submit the details to the Department of National Revenue for consideration and ultimate approval. If I use the word "approval", I think my hon. friend will know what I mean. I refer only to approval for tax deduction purposes. To the extent that the plan comes forward for consideration before in fact there is a tax deduction, it would seem to me that "register" covers to some extent at least what we are trying to say. It is much better than "approved"; and I think we ought to continue to use the word "registered".
We use the word "file" with respect to returns and that is a satisfactory word. We never talk about registering returns of taxpayers.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: No.

What happens with respect to these approved pension plans? In the first place, application is made for approval of the plan. Certain documents are submitted. We will say that a new plan comes into effect, initiated by the employer and employee, and it is filed. Then the department

Income Tax Act
each year may require the filing ot all the information that is required. Surely the actual step is closely akin to the filing of a return or other information that the department has the right to exact. This is not a case of registration at all. I think it is a most unhappy expression that is being coined now for this purpose.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I think my hon. friend omits one factor with regard to registration, namely the decision of the Department of National Revenue that the plan is one in connection with which tax deduction may be granted. If we use the word "file", as the hon. member indicates, it would only mean that we would have some kind of filing case in which we would put the plan and use it accordingly. The matter goes further than that. It goes to the extent of approval, if you will, for this purpose. There must be some action taken by the Department of National Revenue other than mere filing.

Without trying to pursue the matter beyond proper limits, may I say this. I think what the minister has done now is to make out a case for the retention of the present expression in the act. He has not made out a case for introducing an expression like "registered pension". He has made out a case for retaining the word "approved". Where is the difficulty? Who is being misled by the present expression?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I do not know who is being misled, Mr. Chairman, but I know I was misled when I read the act. Anyone who reads it could readily come to the conclusion that the Department of National Revenue had approved that particular pension plan, and that that approval could extend to the terms of it, to whether it is wise or unwise or whether it is desirable or otherwise for the employee. We want to avoid having any such suggestion made.

Is that not true? Is that not a fact? The department does not approve plans the terms of which are not satisfactory, does it? I think the minister is being a little bit squeamish about the effect or the use of the word "approved".

Just before we go on, Mr. Chairman, there are a couple of questions I should like to get cleared up in my own mind. Whose responsibility is it going to be to set a value on these benefits? That is the first question. Then in the case of the automobile that was cited as an example by the minister, is it necessary that the automobile be registered in the name of the taxpayer in order for it to be deemed to be taxable as income? if it is kept in the name
[Mr Fbiring.f
of the company I do not see how it can be taxable, unless it is transferred as private property.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: As to the former question, the valuation would, of course, be one which ultimately, if not decided between the taxpayer and the assessor, would have to be determined by the courts, or by the assessment that may be made. But in any cases such as those mentioned by my hon. friend there would have to be some preliminary discussion between the parties concerned. I would really think in the latter case it really does not matter who is the registered owner of the motor vehicle. It depends on the facts of the case as to whether the employee receives the use of a motor car from the employer, which is of a certain value to him.

Mr. Chairman, the Minister of National Revenue has many times claimed that he and his department insist upon following the letter of the act and that they are only a collection agency. Under the department of the Minister of Finance the terms of the act are actually determined, and it is up to the Department of National Revenue to collect in full. The minister has even gone so far as to say that in his estimation some of the provisions of the act may appear unjust, but he cannot do anything about it. He and his department must insist upon collecting every penny that they say the act calls for, if it is left to the Department of National Revenue to make up their minds.
The minister says it is not the intention to collect on the uniforms of firemen and that type of thing. However, I do not think there is going to be any alternative, once this becomes law and gets into the hands of the Department of National Revenue, to doing what the Minister of National Revenue says has to be done. They are going to contend that their hands are tied. The decision as to every last detail of any kind whatsoever, as it says here, is going to be in the hands of the tax department.
The minister has admitted that he has not had any great difficulty. There was some small doubt in a small incident, or something of that nature, but he has admitted that he has not had any case go to the appeal board in any instance. As a consequence it would be much better if the wording of the act were left as it is at the moment and the taxpayer were given the small benefit of whatever doubt there may be.

speakerposition: Minister of Defence Production; Minister of Trade and Commerce
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, in regard to the question of the use of motor cars by employees of certain organizations, how would that affect people who were working for the dominion government and the provincial governments, which provide

them with motor cars which they use sometimes for their own private purposes. Will the governments pay these people additional wages to look after the income tax they have to pay on the use of the cars.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: It will depend, Mr. Chairman, on the arrangement with the employer as to whether or not the employee may use the car for his own personal purposes to any great extent.

It is well known all over the country that those employees use those cars for their own purposes. Just what percentage of the time they use them is pretty hard to determine, and what the minister is doing in this section is putting into the hands of the assessor, under the Income Tax Act and under the income tax department, the right to decide. He will make an arbitrary decision, such as is being done now all around this country, especially with regard to farmers and others. These people will find that they simply cannot afford to go to court. I think it is quite a vicious section, and it should be reconsidered.

In regard to this matter of the use of motor cars, may I ask the minister what attitude the government proposes to take if this section is enacted in a case where a man is picked up at his residence and is transported to his place of business and vice versa at his employer's expense. Is that benefit to be treated as a part of his taxable income, and will some value be placed upon it by the assessor?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, the question has not arisen in that particular form that I know of. To answer the question asked earlier by an hon. member, I think there is some misunderstanding. I am not aware of any federal employees using motor cars for their own benefit. If they are I think it is contrary to the regulations.

Let me put the case. The minister has not answered my point. I would think the minister would have to answer that. I was referring to the use of a motor car or to motor car privileges that are used as an example to justify the extension of the present legislation. Take the case of a senior officer of the Department of National Defence, for instance, who is picked up at his residence and transported to the offices of the department in a government car. Is that to be regarded as a benefit on which a value is to be placed by the assessor and added to that officer's income, and be subjected to taxation?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Mr. Chairman, the purpose of the discussion on motor cars was to cover the case where a motor car was placed at the
Income Tax Act
disposal of an employee and used by him to his own advantage. The case my hon. friend has stated is one of a company providing some kind of bus service or transportation service for that employee, which is a wholly different matter.

The minister has not dealt with my example of a senior officer being transported to the offices of the Department of National Defence to carry out his daily duties there. Take again the comparable example of an executive who is picked up by a motor car owned by a corporation and driven by a chauffeur of the corporation, in which he is transported from his place of residence to his place of business and then brought back again at night. Is that to be treated as taxable income? I really cannot see much difference in the two cases. If there is a tax payable in the case of the corporation executive, I fail to distinguish the difference in the case of the senior officer who is transported in a government car from his home to the offices of the Department of National Defence.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: I would be inclined to agree with my hon. friend that there is no distinction; but, as I say, I am not aware of any case where a company sends a car to pick up a person and brings him in and that person is charged income tax on that benefit.

No, not now, but we are talking about a case that is going to exist if this section is enacted, and the minister has put his whole case for this wide extension of the meaning of income in this situation on these motor car privileges. Now, surely, the test is not to be the fact that the man has the motor car in his possession and drives it himself. Surely the test is whether there are motor car advantages or benefits made available to him as an incident or term of his employment.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: Well, that is the very point, and the mere fact that a company would send a car to pick up an employee would not, I think, come under the case where we are thinking in terms of assessing persons for the use of a motor car as such and not just the use of the car for a trip to work or something of that kind.
What would be the position of the Minister of Finance?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext: The Minister of Finance does not pay income tax on his motor car allowance.

Mr. Chairman, what the minister has just said is quite the opposite of the practice of the department, because

Income Tax Act one of the things the department has insisted upon is that an employee is not permitted to have the advantage of transportation from his place of residence to his place of employment. It is directly opposite to what the department has practised.

In all earnestness I am going to suggest to the minister, in the light of the discussion we have had tonight, that he reconsider this clause before the bill comes up again. These are very broad words, "of any kind whatsoever"; indeed, they are as broad, I think the minister will agree, as any draftsman can write. I do not think there is a member in this house tonight who can foresee the full application of these words. I earnestly urge upon the minister that before this bill comes up again he reconsider the breadth of his words and see if there is not something that admits of a much clearer definition and understanding than those words.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
speechtext:
Perhaps I am at fault in some respects, but I am afraid I cannot go along
with the thought that the words are not clear and understandable.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall the clause
carry?
No; it is ten o'clock.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext:
Shall I report progress and ask leave to sit again.
Clause stands.
Progress reported.

In that order?
